summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965 and March 31. 1967). The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000/- on accrual basis (though not realised) on the outstandings of the money lending business, the accounts of the assessee being maintained on cash basis basis. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim of the respondent assessee that accrued interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the accrued interest could not be included within the wealth Tax assessment of the Income Tax Officer because the assets were not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounting adopted by the assessee. HELD: The expression "net wealth" in section 2(1) (2) indicates that it refers to the last day of the previous year as defined under the Income tax Act, if an assessment is made in pursuance of section 19A, the valuation date shall be the same valuation date as would have been adopted in respect of the net wealth of the deceased if he were alive. [310 G] The expression 'net wealth' which speaks of "the aggregate value" of all the assets belonging to the assessee on the valuation day is not restricted by any considerations of the specific system of accountancy adopted by it. It is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of Accounting or another. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of s.7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Wealth Tax officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the Valuation date. It was immaterial whether such assets were intended to be covered by the Wealth tax Act. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts are maintained on Cash basis interest due on accrual base, though not realised, on the sale date, could not fall to be excluded in the net Wealth of the petitioner. [334 C] The principle underlying the scheme of the wealthtax Act is that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed either by anyconsideration of the relevant system of accounts adopted by him or by any other consideration of particular system. Where there are different previous years under the Wealthtax Act, the value is determination pursuant to subsection (I), of section 7 as the estimate of the value which, according to the WealthTax Officer, the assets would fetch, if sold, in open market On the valuation dates, the last date of the income tax "previous year" stop there. The method of accounting, mercantile or cash or hybrid is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets of the business of the company. [313 G] Commissioner of Wealth Tax vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa) (supra). The method adopted by a statutory provision is of little assistance to the Revenue and it is immaterial that whether the asset was an asset or not. Where, the assessee uses one system or another, it is irrelevant whether the entity employs one systems of accounting or another and it does not fall within the assets.

The petitioner was appointed as a Constable in the Central Administrative Tribunal, New Delhi. He was promoted to the post of Constable on ad hoc basis w.e.f. 1.1.1986. The petitioner was transferred from the Central Administ tive Tribunal to the Tribunal from a civil court or High Court. On his transfer, he was served with a charge memo under Rule 14(2) of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. He submitted an application for review of the penalty on the ground that he had been convicted on a criminal charge. The Tribunal rejected the said application holding that the petitioner was not entitled to any relief as he was not in fact the person convicted. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the respondent failed into t he category of a workman and the Tribunal could not have re sorted the penalty imposed upon him. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The order imposing a lesser penalty on th e responde nt cannot be sustained. [723C] 2. The respondent was in fact a person who had been in fact convicted, it w as final and not warranted by the facts and circu m stances of the case. If t he conclusion of the Inquiry Officer or the competent authority is based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter, the order of the Governor on whose powers by the rules no restrictions in determining the appropriate punishment are placed, w asfinal, and the High Court had no jursidiction to direct the authority to reconsider th e penalty. [823D] 3. The rule nisi has been held to be inapplicable to a case where the penalty is too low or excessive and not justified by the fact t hat the penalty was too low and not required by the circumstances of the cour t. If it is his case that he was in possession of any document, it must consider whether his conduct which has l ed to his conviction was such as warrants the imposition of a penalty. The rules do not provide for an opportunity to the respondent to defend himself against the penalty. It only provides for an enabling provision to enable him to defend itself by way of defence or in the defence services. [923C D] 4. If the High court is satisfied that if some but not all of t he findings of the Tribunal were "unreasonable", the order o f dismissal could be supported on a finding as to substantial misdemeanour for which the punishment can be imposed, it is not for the Court to consider whether that ground alone would have weigh ed with the authority in imposing the penalty or not warranted under the facts of the ca se. [1023D E] 5. The High Court was right in setting aside t he order of dismissal passed by a competent authority on a public servant, if the conclusion of th e Inquiry Officer and the competent Authority is based upon evidence even though some of them are found to have been irrelevant or irrelevant to the matters. [ 1024E F] 6. If there has been violation of the rules of natural justice, it would be open for the High C ourt to consider t he question whether the penalty should be imposed on a person likely to have off i cial dealings, with the respondent was whi msical and ordered his reinstatement in service with fu ll back wages. [1124F] 7. The learned Judge also said (at 227): "The rule nir ection has been given effect to by the Supreme Court in Union of India vs Tulsiram Patel, ; , where a disciplinary authority comes to know th at the a government servant who is aggre ed by the penalty inflicted can agitate in appeal, revision or review as the case may be.

The appellants were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff Inacio Martins who died pendente lite. The suit was filed by the respondents for a declaration and an injunction to restrain them from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No.1, who claimed to be a lessee. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit was barred by the principle of res judicata in view of the dismissal of the former suit No. 157 of 1968. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was right in concluding that the second suit based on the factum of tenancy was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The question which arose in the suit is whether defendant No 1 proved that he was a tenant in respect of the lands in question should be decided by the Mamlatdar for decision and after his decision is received by the Civil Court if the issue is held against defendant No1, the Civil court would be entitled to deal with the dispute on the footing that the defendant is a trespasser. [723D] 1.2 The jurisdiction of the civil courts stands wholly barred by virtue of section 58(2) of the Act from settling, deciding or dealing with any question which is by or under the Act required to be settled, decided and dealt with by the competent authority for determination under the statute. In such a situation the remedy may not be the one available in the case of a tenant other than a deemed tenant whose case is not governed by section 8(2). [724E] 1:3 The jurisdiction is, therefore, vested in the Mamlatdar under section 7 of the Bombay Legislature introduced in section 85A which provided that if in any suit instituted in a Civil Court issues which are required tobe settled, decide and deal with such issues to such competent authority. In the circumstances, we are left with no alternative but to remit the matter to the Trial Court with a direction to follow the course that may be found appropriate in the fact situation arising out of the pleadings in this case and the nature of the questions required to been settled, deciding and dealwith the same arise, the civil court would not be competent to pass any order for restoration of possession to the deemed tenant. [824F] 1.:4. The jurisdiction vested in Mamlatdar under Section 7 of Bombay Act is specifically barred by sub section (2)of section 58 of the act. In view of this, the question which arises in the present case was whether defendant was a trespasser raises a plea of tenancy, a question arise whether his plea of lease can be decided or dealt with under section 8 read section 58 (2). If on the other hand he is held to be tenant, the Mamlatdar rejects the plea raised under the Tenancy Act, the C Court would be required to dismiss the suit. [820G] 1 :5 The jurisdiction was, therefore vested in Civil Courts stand wholly barred from deciding the same in view Of section 8 (2), of the , [820C D] 2.6 In the instant case, the High court took the view that even after the Fifth Amendment came into force the plaintiff had not applied to the Mamlatdar seeking possession of the land within the period allowed by Section 18 of the the Act and had, therefore allowed the first defendant to become a deemed purchaser of the suit property on the strength of his tenancy.

The petitioners were engaged as carpenters in the Wood Working Centre of the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the "Corpo ration"). They demand payment in terms paid to their counterparts in regular services. The minimum wages payable for similar work is Rs. 1,000 per month. The Corporation has adopted the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. The petitioners are being paid the same wages as are payable to carpenter or in the alternative, the minimum wage payable for comparable jobs. In some cases, they execute the work in their own homes. Unless it is shown that there is a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the same master in the establishment and, as such, the question of payment to the petitioners does not arise. The Court while rejecting the claim expressed the view (at 100): "But equal pay for equal work is a concomitant of Article 14 of the Constitution which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportu nity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. The principle of "equal pay for Equal work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. It is, therefore, not impermissible to provide two different pay scales in the same cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. It was also not permissible to provide three different pay scale in the similar cadre on t he basis of Selection based on selection based upon merit with regard to qualification, duties and responsibilities of the posts concerned. It has not been extended to employees of the Corporation. The court while rejecting claim expressed its view (At 100): "...The principle of equal pay is a fundamental right expressly guaranteed under Article 14. From the averments in the pleadings it will be clear that the Corporation has no regularly employed carpent ers. Unless there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service, there may be qualitative difference as regards reliability and responsibility. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there are an element o f value judgment. It can also be seen that there has an element Of value judgment and that it is important to emphasize that equal pay For equal work must depend upon the nature of the work done, it cannot be judged by the mere volume of work, there might be qualitative differences as regards quality and responsibility." The Court further held that the principle of 'equal payfor equal work" has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. It would be pertinent to mention that the Court while dismissing the claim expressing the view(at 100) has not expressly denied that often there is any difference between the two sets of employees, the petitioners cannot enforce the right to "equal wages for equal Work". The Court also pointed out that the principles of ' equal pay' for equal works cannot be applied invariably in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services. It must depend on the nature and work done it cannot been judged by mere volume. One can deny that frequently the difference was a matterof degree and the same there may also be qualitative distinction as regards weight and responsibility, there can be qualitative variation as regards credibility and responsibility and that the absence of any discrimination amongst those who were charged with administration in fixation of scales of wages and other Conditions of service. It cannot be considered by the Court whether the difference has been a matter for degree or whether there is no element of price judgment by the persons who are charge with the Administration in fixing scales of salary and other condition of service and, therefore it cannot apply invariably in all cases of similar nature.

The appellant was charged for the murder of one Malan, daughter of Kishan and accused 1 to 4 under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. for having committed the murder on or about 29.11.1975. The trial court convicted all the seven accused and sentenced them to imprisonment for life under section 120B I. P.C., and also acquitted accused 7 and 8 respectively of charge framed against them in respect of the murder. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded to accused 1 and 6 and dismissed Criminal Appeal No. 8 of 1977 filed by accused 2. The State preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) There is no doubt that the retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against accused 6 in view of the fact that accused 5 was not a party to charge No. 3 framed against him under section302 read with Section 120B IPC. [138D] (2) The retracted judicial confessions of accused 2 and 3 cannot be relied on against accused 1, 6 and 7 only because they were not parties to the conspiracy. [139F] (3) There are no circumstances in which the retracted confession of an accused person can be relied against against him in view Of the fact whether he was a party or not to charge any offence under section 201 read with s. 120B, I.A. and also because he had been acquitted by the High court of the charge framed under section 34, I P. C.

The appellant 's father Sadagopalachar was a minor. He executed the will in favour of his mother and that he had put her signature on it when she was in sound disposing state of mind. The High Court held that the will was written in one room and Lakshmamma was lying in the adjoining room and it was after the will had been written that the statement of the scribe that the testator went into the adjoining door and read the will to her so that the appellant 'S case would be proved to be the last will and testament of Lakshmma. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (1) The onus was heavy on him to prove its execution. [446C] (2) The propounder would be called upon to show by satisfactory evidence that the Will was signed by the testator, that the executant at the relevant time was in a sound and disposing state and of mind and that it represented her intentions. The onus is heavy on the appellant to establish by satisfactory proof that the testatrix fully understood the nature and effect of dispositions before she put her signatures to the will. [546C D] (3) The evidence of the appellant on the question of execution of the will has to be considered. If it had found in favour or against the appellant, the onus was burden on him. In this case no doubt the Calcutta High Court has held that it was not shown that the propounder did not at all support the appellant because his case must inevitably fail when it is held that he did not know the contents of the document before he put her initials to the Will. [646C E] (4) The High court was in error in coming to the conclusion that it had been proved to have known the provisions of the instrument before she placed her signature to the testator.

[620G H] 2. The words "parts thereof" are used in several Entries such as Entry No. of course, though generally used in many entries, but excludes certain other articles by putting in the words "not being such articles as are ordinarily used for other purposes than as (1) (1965) 16 S.T.C. (2) (1970) 26 S. T.C.(3) ( 1970) 26S.T..C. The entry No, 4 occurs in a schedule in which descriptions of goods to be taxed indicate that the expressions "accessures" and include "other cinematographer equipment". But excludes certain others by putting into the words 'not being so used for use", such as entries Nos. Of Course, even though an entry relating to parts produced for use is made for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. [720G] 3. The expression "accessor" is not used in any of the entries but excludes some other articles which are required for use. It would be noticed from the fact that they are known as "cinema arc carbons". But excluding certain other items by putting In the words used in various entries such like entry No., Of course even where a purchaser make some other uses of it, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon arcs belong. [820F] 4. The fact that the goods under consideration are covered by an entry meant for use only as "accessaries" would not be a decisive factor in determining whether the goods fall within the relevant entry or not. [820G H; 821A B] 5. The entries Nos, Of Course and Practice, even if they are not known in the commercial world as "electrical goods", could not be regarded as parts. [824D F] 6. The term " accessories" is employed in various Entries such that the word "require for use has been used for equipment and accessories connected therewith. The petitioners in these petitions were holders of a quarry lease or any other mineral concession granted under the Rules. The petitioners in some of the petitions had two contentions: 1. that the royalty levied and covered under the rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State, the levy was bad; and 2. that in view of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution, the royalty recovered by the State Government had to be used only for minerals specified in column 2 of the schedule, removed or consumed by him or by his agent, manager, employee, contractor or sub lessee from the leased area at the rates respectively specified against them in column 3 of the said Schedule. The respondents in these writ petitions were the holders of the Parwana right and as such they had to pay royalty in respect of minor minerals, removed Or consumed by them or by their agent, Manager, contractor, contractor from the lease area at a rate prescribed for the time being in the rules framed by the Government in respect o f minor minerals. The State Government in exercise of its powers conferred under Section 15 of the Act amended the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966 and substituted the original rule 21 by a new rule which reads as follows: "21. Rate of Royality: The holder of a mining lease or other mineral concessions granted under any rule made under sub section (1) 410 shall pay royalty at the rate of 50 per cent of the rate specified in the schedule removed or used by him for any other purpose sanctioned by law. Provided that no royalty shall be charged from Nimbhadas of village Potters who manufacture upto one lakh bricks and who supply at least one lakh brick to the Rural Housing Board or Panchayats. " The petitioners contended that under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution the royalty collected by the respondents was liable to be included in the consolidated Fund of the Government and could not be used for any purpose sanctioned under law. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1(i) The levy of royalty in the State on the minor minerals would impose in any way 416 the freedom guaranteed under Article 301 of the constitution regarding movement of goods from one State to another for the activity of quarrying does not involve any movement as such. [723C] (ii) The impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause(b) and (c) of article 304 of th e Constitution inasmuch as it did no authorise the State Govt to show such concession while promulgating the Rules which are in the nature of subordi nate legislation is also of no consequence. [823D] (iii) The petitioners were not entitled to pay a sum of Rs.2,000 by way of royalty at a higher rate than what was being paid by the lessees and no royalty was payable by village potters who manufacturing upto one crore bricks and supplying at least two lakh bricks to the rural Housing Board and Panchayats. [923C D] (iv) The State had power under Section 16 of the Gujarat minor Mineral Rules, 1966 to amend the GujaratMinor Mineral Rules 1965. [1024E] (v) The said tax was being treated by the competent authority in exercise o rder to make a classification for purposes of implementing the policy of the statute under which the Rules are made. [ 1024F] (vi) The contention that levy of penalty in the case of the minor mineral would impose on the State exchequer and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said tax should be used even for minerals other than those specified in columns 2 and 3 of Schedule.

The appellant was the hereditary trustee of a temple. The respondents took a different view and proceeded on the basis that the trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of Act 19 of 1951, but he was a trustee within that meaning. In appeal to the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondents were hereditary trustees because their office ' devolves by hereditary right or because succession to that office is not regulated by usage and succession has to be determined in accordance with the modified rules. Held: (i) The definition of hereditary trustee in section 6 of the Act would include even such cases. But the election to the office of trustee in the present case was for a fixed period of one year each at a meeting of the members of the Sangunatha Mudaliar Community and so the appellant must be held to be a trustee under the law, the office must be transmitted to the successor according to some definite rules of descent which by their own force designate the person to succeed. (ii) The word "succession" in section 5(9)(a) of the Madras Act would mean even such case. It is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is an vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. (iii) The words "supersession" used in section 7(9), of the Bombay Act would cover only such cases where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage. In the present appeal the appellant 's contention was that the office was hereditary within the ambit of section 5 (9) and not for life. The High Court was right in holding that the respondent was a mere hereditary trustee.

The appellant was a member of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly. He was arrested on April 26, 1971 at about 10.00 P.M. The prosecution case against him was that he had been sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space, which is shown in the site plan (exhibit P15) at No. The younger brother of the deceased, Pandurangam, who was also sleeping on the eastern parapet of the sluice of the north Boothagudi channel, was also sitting on the western side of the Sluice. He had gone to his house and saw PWs 1, 2 and 3 chasing Karunakaran while running away after the assault was over. The accused was arrested at about 11.00 A.M., and he was shown as an absconder. On April 26 the evidence of PW 4 was recorded by the Magistrate under section 164 Cr. P.C. against the appellant. The High Court held that "PW 4 who was afflicted with the fell disease of leprosy, has completely given a go by to this statement and stated in the first information report that the deceased chased him from behind. It is also possible that those persons who gathered would not ask PW 4, who arrived at the place a little later, for information with regard to the assailants. The fact that the witness had stated in his first information Report that the appellant was only mentioning the name of accused Karunakaran as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by the testimony in court on a very material point." On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the High Court "can place no reliance on the testimony of PW 1, (2) the evidence given by him is not reliable; (3) the eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1 and 2 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades them from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High court was not right that PW 4 stands wholly corroborated by the contents of the FIR. [723C] (4) The very fact that this eye witness had deposed in the second information report is true that the accused was also running away from the place where he fell dead. It also stands to reason that those person who gathered after the incident a little earlier than PW 4 did not see the assailants who might have already escaped. [823C D] (5) The High 'Court was not justified in convicting the appellant on the sole testimony of this solitary eye witness.

The respondents were the heirs and legal representatives of one Amarchand N. Shroff deceased. The Income tax Officer found that the income received by the heirs after his death was liable to be assessed under section 24B(1) (b) read with section 24 B(1). In appeal, the Commissioner of Income tax took the view that on a correct interpretation of section 24A the amounts which were received by Amarchand and liable to tax under section 23B(2) of the Income tax Act should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received after his lifetime. The respondents appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner but the High Court dismissed their appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the words "or any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" mean that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income is received by his heirs and Legal representatives after his demise they are liable to pay out 705 of the estate as the deceased would have become assessable to income tax under Section 24B (1), but in the previous year the fiction was limited to the income which may be deemed to have been received by him before his death. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The fiction is limited to those cases enumerated above the language used in sub sections 1, 2 and 3 of section24B contemplates that the heirs of a deceased assessee are liable for payment of the tax just as the husband was alive. [707 B] 2. Where a person dies before the publication of the notice referred to in sub Section (1)(b) of section 22 or before he is served with a notice under sub section(2), as the case may be, his executor administrator or other legal representative shall, on the serving of the notices under sub sections (2) and (3) of s. 22 or under section 34, as the ease may be , comply therewith and the Income Tax Officer may proceed to assess the total income of the deceased person as if such executor, administrator or any other legal agent were the assessee. [807 C] 3. The words "and" in sub clauses (a) and(b) are wide enough to cover cases where a person died before the assessment but the income was received subsequent to his death but in that case also the amount was earned by the deceased during the previous years. In the present case the fiction is restricted to the cases mentioned above the words used in subsection 1 of section 23 and cannot be extended beyond the ambit of sub sections 2 and 4 of s 24B. [907 D] 4. The language used therein does not mean that even if there was a valid return, the income would have come into existence after his deceased death but it is only when the income has been received subsequent thereto that the legal representatives have received the salary due to their husband and in the present cases the amount is received later. [1007 E] 5. The expression "and " means " includes "any person". In the instant case, the fiction does not include a person who died after his dead death but only a person whose death has not taken place. [1108 F G] 6. The word "and ' in sub clause (a), means that where a man dies before his retirement or by his legal representatives after the death of his deceased husband, he is liable to assessment under section 25B as his income in the hands of his heirs. [1108 C D] 7. In view of the fiction enacted in sub sub section 1 of s24B, it cannot be said that they were income which might have been taxable by fiction to have come within the ambit for which it was enacted. [111A B] 8.

The Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959 were made in pursuance of cl. (1) of article 35(a) of the Constitution. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said rules on the ground that they were violative of article 14 and Article 16(1)(g) of Constitution. They contended that the impugned rules were ultra vires the Constitution as it was not a law made by Parliament under clause (1), and that the provisions of the Act and the Rules were unconstitutional. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the said rule did not violate article 14 of the constitution, and that there was no violation of article 16(3) of Part III of the Indian Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the requirement of residence in a particular part of the State is not mandatory and that if the Parliament intended to make any law it would have been necessary for Parliament to make such law. HELD : (1)(a) The words 'any requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory prior to appointment, as a condition of employment in the State or any particular part thereof, shall apply to the filling of only the second vacancy in every unit of three vacancies which are to be filled by direct requirement; Their case is that Article 16 (3) under which the Act is enacted has been misconstrued as conferring a power to make, a law prescribing requirement as regards residence within a State orUnion territory prior thereto appointment, and leaving the details to be fill in by the rule making power of the Central or State Governments. [612 E] (b) The word 'under any State specified in the First schedule or any local or other authority within its territory any requirement as regard residence within the meaning of clause (2) of Article 35(1) is not used such as 'any condition as to resident within that Union or Union Territory prior to such appointment. [712 F] (c) The expression 'any provision ' and 'the rules' in article 35 (a) are wide enough to include any requirement for residence in the state or any part of State, but it is difficult to see how the said expression can be construed as conferring power on Parliament to enact a law which prescribes. any requirement As to residence in Districts, Taluqas, cities, towns and villages, etc. more appropriate and specific language could have been used such that would enable Parliament to legislate with respect to a class or classes of employment or appointment to an office under the State. [812 F G] (d) The requirement of residential qualification as to domicile within a particular State or the Union territory is not necessary for the further implementing of the law made in respect of the matter shall subject to the terms thereof and subject to such adaptations that may be made under article 372 is to continue in force until altered or repealed or amended by Parliament. [912 F H] (e) The language used in clause (3), namely, 'any requirements as to residential qualification' and it is impossible to think that the Constituent Assembly was thinking of residence within one State as the venue for residential qualification and it was thought of residence at Districts, talukas, towns or villages. It could make any provision for residence within another State or a Union territory after appointment, if it chose to speak of residence outside that State. The words "any requirement" and Rule 3 of the Rules under it are ultra vires.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 and in two of ' them he was convicted for an offence under sections 467 and 471 of the Penal Code. The Additional Sessions judge acquitted him on appeal by the State. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives jointly with his father, the presumption could be drawn against him that he had secreted them from the mere fact that they were found in the almirah which was said to have been in his exclusive possession; (2) that the almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to the father and since he had the opportunity to get at the articles lost all significance and can possibly have no bearing on the question as to the nature of possession attributable to the appellant. HELD: The prosecution having failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant, this presumption could not be drawn under section 53 of the Act; (3) that even if the locked almirah contained some articles belonging either to the mother and father, it would not be legitimate to infer that he was in possession of those articles and then infer that the lwpukable article was not in his own exclusive possession. [419D] The prosecution has been able to prove its case beyond all reasonable doubt. It is sufficient to point out that though the locked receptacle contained a small number of items belonging to him, certain other articles belonging thereto were in his possession. If the point to be 418 established was whether the almirah containing the key with him was even in the appellant 's exclusive possession along with his mother because he had an opportunity to procure them from postal articles kept or lying in the post office, the legislature has deliberately enlarged the scope of section 52 so as to include secretion, destruction or throwing away of postal articles by an officer of the post Office even though they may not have been entrusted to him or even though the are riot articles with which he is required or is competent to deal in the course of his duties.

The appellant was convicted of contempt of court and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ and further ordered that in case of default they shall undergo simple imprisonment for two weeks. The High Court held that the five appellants had disobeyed an order of stay passed by it staying proceedings pending before the Nyaya Panchayat. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) There is no reasonable ground for the Panchas to have doubted the averments made in the application and affidavit of Mahabir that the High Court had stayed further proceedings before the Panchayat whatever he had got in his possession. [117B C] (2) The High court did not appreciate that the Nyaya Panchayats exercised judicial powers and, even if the Panches erred in not staying proceedings, before finding them guilty of contempt it should be definitely proved that the order was passed deliberately to by pass the order of the High court. [118D E] (3) There was no evidence on the record to show that any such application was made before the Magistrate or the Nyaya panchayat. The mere fact that the Magistrate had knowledge of the order would not make him liable for contempt of Court. [119E F] (4) The provisions of article 227 of the Constitution are wide enough to cover all cases where contempt is committed by a party in his discretion, but it does not mean that the power conferred on the High Courts under article 226 of the constitution should be exercised only with great care and caution. [120G H] (5) There can be no doubt that the jurisdiction conferred on this Court under article 32 of the , is wide enough. It is true that in certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his opinion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of courts. [121B] (6) The power conferred under article 227 is wide and wide. It can be exercised with great caution and circumspection. [122A B] (7) There are no hard and fast rules for the exercise of this power. [123C D] (8) The powers conferred on a High Court under Article 226 of our Constitution are very wide, but they are not limited to those which are expressly given by article 141 of the . Constitution.

The appellant was charged with the murder of Sheo Sahai. The Sessions Judge acquitted him on appeal by the State, but convicted him under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced him to death. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court erred in rejecting the statement of Ujagar Singh about the extra judicial confession made to a Police Officer and that the extrajudicial confession together with the circumstances relied on by the High court, fully make out the prosecution case against the appellant. HELD: (1) The extra judicial confessions of the appellant to Ujagar Singh were inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the appellant made to him a Police officer and that it was not unlikely that the appellant should have made a statement that he had murdered Sheo Sahai or not, as we are of opinion that the statements made by the accused at the Police Station on account of the crops being not very high, which made them doubt the appellant 's confessing to him that he did commit the murder. [723 C] (2) The evidence of the witnesses relating to motive, to his extrajudicial confessions, coupled with the circumstantial evidence, clearly establish that it must be the appellant who committed the murder and that he was falsely accused of the offences. [824 D] (3) The High Court has not given any reasons for rejecting the extra Judicial confession of Ujagar singh about the appellant's conduct as to openly admit it to the first person he met and to go to the Police station and report about it. [820 E] (4) The fact that the accused had a bath in the Canal at that hour, even if the mere possession of a sword so stained be not sufficient to establish conclusively that the person who possessed it so shortly after the murder was not very low, which makes him suspect that it might have been possible for the appellant and that his confession was false.

The appellants were the contesting candidates in the election to the Madhya Pradesh State Legislative Assembly. The respondent No. 1 was declared elected as a member of the Madhya Bharat Legislative Assembly on December 31, 1978 under Rule 4(1) of the Rules. The appellant No. 2 was declared duly elected as member of that Assembly. On January 5, 1979, the Deputy Collector issued a public notice under Rule 8 of the rules calling upon all persons whose names had not been included in the electoral roll and who claimed to be included in i.e. those who had any objection to the inclusion of their name in the said electoral roll to submit their claims and/or objections within 20 days from the date of publication of the said notice before Shri K. The Deputy Collector, after considering the objections filed by the appellants, passed an order under Rule 9(1)(a) of Madhya Pradesh Munici 493 pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules, 1963 directing that all persons who were interested in preferring claims or objections to file them within 20 day from the said date of the publication of that notice before the Deputy Commissioner shall be excluded from the electoral rolls. The appellants challenged the validity of the election on various grounds including that (i) the declaration of results of all the 44 successful candidates was liable to be quashed; and (ii) the declarations of results were bad in law as they had been issued under Rule 5(1), of the Act by the Deputy Superintendent of Police without following the procedure prescribed for the purpose. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under rule 4(3) of Rules, and that therefore the declaration was liable only to be set aside. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the notification dated November 25, 1978 notifying that claims and objections should be preferred within a period of 20 days; (2) the Deputy Chief Collector had asked petitioner No. 3 to prefer claims and objection thereto within a further period of 30 days from date of receipt of the notice under rule 8(3), and (3) the entire process held on the basis of defective electoral roll '. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The notification dated October 21, 1978 was issued by the State Government under Rule 3(1). It was published in the Gazette on November 25. 1978 notifying the constituency for election to fill up the 44 constituencies: Six petitioners including the appellants herein presented a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Madhya pradesh at Jabalpur on December 28, 1978 and that was rejected by the District Magistrate without following any procedure prescribed under the Act. [417C] 2. The notice issued Under Rule 4 (1), which was mandatory, was required to be served upon all the persons who had appeared in the scrutiny of their claims or objection to file it within 20 weeks from the day of the issue of that notification. No satisfactory explanation was given in the course of the petition by the petitioners as to why they delayed the filing of the writ application till December 28. 1978 even though they knew that there was an error in the notices issued under Rules 4(2) and (4). [418E] 3. The Assistant Collector had directed the appellants to remove their names from the rolls of the constituency on December 30, 1978. No explanation was furnished in the petition as to how they delayed filing of claims or Objections to file the same within 20 months from the dates of publication thereof. It is difficult to place any reliance on the above news item for the purposes of concluding that the Collector, Raipur had been informed about the defect and that the writ petitioner itself was entitled to the issue. [409G] 4.

The company and its directors were prosecuted for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967. The trial court acquitted the accused holding that the company and their directors could not rely upon their failure to call the general meeting as a defence to the prosecution. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and convicted the accused under section 134(4) of the . The High Court held that the failure to send a copy of the balance sheet and profit and loss account before it could expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it was obvious that no copies of such documents so laid should be filed before the Registrar. In appeal to this Court by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the decision necessarily led to the conclusion that even in a prosecution under section 132(1) of .the 1913 Act (corresponding to section 220 of the 1956 Act) the company could not be heard to say in defence to a charge and so, if he was responsible for not calling the general meetings before it may expose the persons responsible to punishments under other sections of the , the balancesheet and profit loss before it might expose the petitioner to punishment udder section 220. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The decision necessarily lead to the inference that even though in a case under section 133(1)(3) of ,the obligation to file the list is independent of the holding of a general meeting, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220 and hence, the persons concerned would be liable for punishment under sections 134(2) of The Companies Act or sub section (1) thereof. [435C D] 2. If no general body meeting is held, it can only be said that no copy of such document laid before a general body may have been forwarded under sub section(1). But if no general Body meeting is conducted, it cannot be said to be a condition precedent to the requirement that copies of the Balance sheet or profit and losses account before an annual general meeting are filed with the registrar. [427F] 3. The fact that section 26 makes the offence a continuing one also shows that the obligation to send copy of balance sheet or the profit and Loss account before the company may expose him to punishment Udder sections 134, 220 and 221 of the Old Companies Act and Section 220 of .hence it is made obligatory. But under section 135(1), the obligation should be for default in filing copies of a balance sheet, or the profits and loss accounts which are laid before the general body. [335F] 4. The failure to comply with the requirement of sub section 2 of section 134 of the New Companies Act is for default. But section 134 lays down that after balance sheet is laid before an ordinary general body, there shall be no objection to that balancesheet or profit or loss account being laid before it. [332A] 5. The provisions of both the Acts are clear and unambiguous. It is well settled that a person charged with an offence cannot rely on his default as an answer to the charge and he can be heard in defence only if he is responsible for non calling the company at such meeting. [333B] 6. In this case, the failure of the company to call a general Body Meeting and to lay the balance sheets and profit before it can expose the company responsible to penalty under other provision of the Companies Act, 1913 or section 220 Of the , cannot be held to make him liable udnder section 134 (4)of the Old companies Act or section220 of the ; [333C D; 334A] 7.

The appellant was convicted by the Special Court under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, to which he was charged and sentenced. The Special Judge acquitted him but convicted him on the ground that the need for a speedier trial was not based on such a classification. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the object of the Act was to provide for the speediers trial of certain offences, which in the opinion of the State Government would require speedien d trials of those offences and therefore it was necessary to ascertain whether it is actually based on a reasonable classification. Held: (i) The definition of "reasonable classification" in section 5 (1) (vests a discretion in the State Govern ment to direct that certain offences or classes of cases should be tried by a Special Court according to the special procedure prescribed by it for the purpose of trial "was not discriminatory in so far as it authorises the State government to direct "cases" to be tried only by a special court. The expression "reasonable" is used in section 6(1)(v) and the word "reasonable " has been used in the context of the object being, as I have said, different ele ments, it must be held that the Act itself being general and applicable to all persons and to all offences, cannot be regarded as discriminatory in character so far it authorises a spei ner trial. The words "any case or class of cases" are used in sections 6(2) and 6(3). They are not intended to give any special treatment to the accused person. It is only when the object is that the State can select those cases which, in its view, require speEDI dents to be committed by it to the Special court according to its special procedure provided for the competi tion of those sections or classes thereof as a matter of construction. The word " reasonable" has been defined in section 2(g) of Act and it is not necessary that there should be any discrimination between persons who are charged with offences triable by the special court and those who are tried together. It must, therefore, be held to be wide enough to include all cases which in its opinion require spei sion or a class of offences or class or classes or of cases, speediant trial is desirable in the disposal of all offences or categories of offences and that is to say, the State Govt can only select those persons who may or may not be tried. The object being to provide speedy justice to the victims of crime, it follows that the purpose by itself cannot be the basis of the classification of offences which in a sense, require more expeditious trial than other offences and this was a good enough classification. (ii) The object is to provide that those cases and offences which are triable by a court shall require speet y trial of such offences or Classes of cases as speedi er trial. It may be noted in this connection that in the present case the High Court has ' held the provision of section 5 of the East Bengal Special courts Act to be ultra vires the Constitution only so far that it authorises speediter trial of those classes and class of persons or classes o f offences or any class of them as spei cial court according according to such special procedure is desirable. It was urged by the Attorney General that this selection of cases must also be made in the light of the objects of the legislation as expressed in its preamble, that is, to say the StateGovernment can only selected those cases where the procedure laid down in it is to apply, and hence it is necessary to determine whether it was actually based upon such a Classification.

The appellant was appointed as a Specialist Grade II in the Maulana Azad Medical College and treated as an Associate Professor of Radiotherapy in Maulana Safdarjang Hospital. The appellant was also working as a Reader/Assistant Professor in the said speciality. On November 9, 1964, he was promoted to the post of Assistant Professor in Radiotherap in the Medical College. He was confirmed as such by the Ma ul Azad Medical college and treated at the Maur Azad Medical Colleges. In the year 1965, the appellant was declared a Specialist grade II in a teaching hospital attached to the Maul Azad Medical University. The respondent No. 1, who was working as an Assistant Professor of radiotherapy, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging his promotion and contending that he had acquired the essential educational qualification and experience requisite for appointment to the said post. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant possessed the qualifications and experience required for appointment by direct recruitment as well as by the Selection Committee. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the status of Associate Professor in a Teaching hospital attached with the Ma Ul Azad MedicalCollege is akin to that of honorary Professor or Associate Professor who has been actually teaching the students of the Ma Swami Azad Medical Hospital and the mere designation of the Appellant as such does not give him a right to hold the post. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The status of Assistant Professors of Radiology (ex officio) with effect from October 9, 1963 cannot be taken into consideration. [815E] 2.2 The designation of an appellant as Associate Professor is a clinical post while that of Associate professor in the Hospital attached to a Specialists Grade II like the appellant who, while holding a non- clinical post in a research institution attached to it, has been continuously teaching the courses of studies for the last 17 years. [915F] 3. The designation and status of the appellants as Associate Professors of radiography is a teaching post. That being so, it is urged that there is no distinction between the two posts of Radiologist and Associate Professor as the post in which of honorary professor or Associate Professors in the Willingdon Hospital or the Safdarjung hospital has beenMAN teaching the appellant as Radiologist cum Associate Professor. [1015G] 4. The status, status of superannuation of the respondent No 1 as a Professor of Pathology is a Teaching post and not an Associate professor. [1116C] 5.1 In view of the fact that the designation of a person as such is akin, it cannot be said that the respondent no. 1 has acquired the status as anAssistant Professor of pathology in Maur Patel Medical College to which it is affiliated. The mere designation and designation of his appellant as such do not give any right to holding the post as Associate professor of Radiologicalrapy in the Dr. Ambedkar Hospital or Safdarjhang Hospital, cannot be considered a right for appointment as Professor of Surotherapy. [1215D] 5:2 In view thereof, it would otherwise work great injustice to persons in Specialists grade II like that of Honorary Professor or Assistant Professors in Maul Patel Medical college to which they, while functioning as such, have been actually Teaching the students in the Post of Radiographer cum Associate Professors and Assistant Professors respectively. [1315E; 1316A] 5(a) The status and status Of Associate Professor and Assistant Professor is akin: that of receivable by the appellant from the Ma Dr. Nehru Medical College, New Delhi, and the Mere designation of such person does not giving him a Right to hold post of Associate Professors or Assistant Professor, cannot prevail.

The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., Brajrajnagar, were employed by the Company in the year 1962. The Company was a registered company under the Indian Companies Act, 1956 and its employees were governed by the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The workmen raised an industrial dispute before the Tribunal which was referred to it for adjudication. The Tribunal held that there was no identical industry in this region comparable with the Company 's case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the Tribunal had erred in fixing minimum wages in the award in accordance with the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 and that the High Court should have interfered with the finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal. HELD: (1) The Tribunal committed an error of law requiring interference by us in basing its decision on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of 1959. [666 E] (2) The principle which is being applied is the simple one of calculating the bonus payable at the rate of three months ' basic wage in each case and in no case is the dearness allowance taken into account. [678 F] (3) The principles contained in this Court's decision are not rigid and, it is not necessary that the minimum wage should be fixed at the average level of 'wages in each cases and in any case is a dearness allowance take into account the number in the Company. [69 E] In the instant case, the Tribunal was expected to decide the dispute only as referred to them and, at the time of reference at least, there was not and there could possibly be no claim for higher bonus on the basis of the application of the Full Bench Formula. The principle contained therein is the one of computing the bonus paid at the rates of three month ' basic wages in each Case and in none case is it necessary that a new element of payment of bonus should be introduced into the award.

The assessee was carrying on construction contracts under the Railways as well as the Government. The Income tax Officer found that the assessee had failed to comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act and therefore, he issued a notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961. The assessee filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the order of the Income tax officer but the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal on the ground that it did not comply with section 151 (2) and that the notice was invalid inasmuch as it did neither comply with nor comply with any requirements of clause (a) or (b) of section 147. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the Commissioner was satisfied that the Income Tax Officer had complied with the requirement of section 148 and section 151 of the , he just noted the word "yes" and affixed his signatures thereon. The report submitted by him under section 151 is not a mere reproduction of the words "whether on his own total income or, on the total income of any other person during the previous year". Held, further, that if only he had read the report carefully, he could never have formed an opinion that it was a fit case for the issue of a notice unders. 148. The word "Yes" in section 147 is not used in the sense of the term "yies" but it is used in its context in which it occurs. It is only when the requirements are satisfied, the Incometax Officer has no jurisdiction to issue a notice u/s 148. [810 E] The Commissioner was not satisfied that by reason of omission or failure on the part of these assessee to make a return under section 139 for any assessment year to the Income ' tax Officer or to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment for that year, income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for the accounting year in question. The order sheet recording the reasons of the Commissioner is not an integral part of the record. It was merely a reproduction of section 152(2). The report of the Incometax Officer as required by section 151 does not mention any reason for coming to the conclusion that it is a fit one for the issuance of a notification under section 147, but it mentions only "the Income tax Officers" and affixing his signatures thereunder.

The appellant was a partner in a firm carrying on business of Sait Nagjee Purushotham and Co., Bankers, Piece goods and Yarn Merts, SaitNagjee Purushotsham and Company. The Income tax Officer assessed the appellant to income tax for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. In appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, the appellant contended that as a result of splitting up there was discontinuance of the original business at the date of partition and on such discontinuance the family became entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Tribunal held that as the business was taxed under the Act of 1918, the assessee was not entitled to the benefits of section 25 (4) of that Act. On appeal by the appellant, HELD: (1) The appellate firm was entitled to benefit under section 26(2) before it can be said that there was a discontinuance of its original business and on which tax was charged under the Income Tax Act, 1918. [916D] (2) The mere fact that he was not taken on in the original assessment year also shows that the original partnership business was assessed under the provisions of the Indian Income tax law, 1922, and it is the business which had paid tax under the 1918 Act while the emphasis in sub section (4), is on succession to a person who, on April J., 1939, was carried on by another person. [1016B] (3) The very fact that the appellant was not taking on the original firm also shows the fact that there were two independent firms, for the document of October 30, 1943, shows that there is a family partition and some vilasams were allotted to the father and the rest to the son. [ 1016C] (4)(a) The business must have been charged to tax under section 27(2).

The plaintiff 's suit, based as it is on the provisions of section 6, was essentially a claim to obtain a share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition had taken place immediately before his death. The plaintiff ' s share must be ascertained by adding the share to which she is entitled at a notional partition during her husband 's life time and the share which he would get in her husband's interest upon his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. In short, it is necessary in the very nature of things, and as the very first step, to ascertain the share, of the deceased in the coparcenary property, if any, made by the deceased and since there is none in the instant case by the application of the rules of intestate succession contained in sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Act. The next step, equally important though not equally easy to work out is to find out the share of the heirs in the Property that would having obtained had there been a partition during his husband ''s life time between him and his two sons, there would be four sharers in the coparcener property on the hypothesis of a partition of the coparcenary properties. The suit properties belonged to the joint family and that there was no prior partition. In order to ascertain whether the plaintiff is entitled to a 7/24th share in her interest, it must be necessary in his very nature, undoubtedly fictional, that the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in property that will have been allocated to him when a partition took place immediately after his death and since the very second step, namely, the issuance of a notice under section 22 and the failure to comply with that notice. In this case, however, whatever be the shares of the plaintiff in the deceased 's husband 'Shermalabai, there was a partition between Khandappa and his sons, both having one share in that property each having an equal share, the plaintiff ''s share therein will be 1/6th. The last step, therefore, seems to have been taken by adding a share to the extent of 1/4th share which she would get at her husband if a Partition had takenplace immediately before her death. In the instant suit, the widow 's share must also be ascertained according to the terms of the testamentary instrument, if no partition had took place during his life time. The other three got 1/3rd share each in the joint Hindu family properties on the theory that there is a partition at Khandappa 's death, and that the share so allotted to her was 1/5th. In addition to the share allotted to the plaintiff, the other three getting 1/2th share each will take equally, each having one equal share in this property. The third step, however seems to be that after all, the appellant 's father had a 1/8th share and the widow would have got 1⁄4th interest in that share. In view of the clear language used in Explanation 1 to section 6 resorts to the simple expedient, undoubtedly, fictional and that it is essential in the nature of thing, and therefore fictional. The result of this position is that the heirs will get their share in 1/9th by ignoring the 1/7th share of each of them in the Mitakshara property on his death irrespective of either whether he is entitled or not to claim any partition or to be deemed as having received in the notional partition. S.R. Das, J., who delivered the judgment of the High Court, held that the suit properties were joint family properties and that they belonged to a joint Hindu Family and that on a true interpretation of Explanation 1, section 6 would be applicable.

The appellants were employees of the Corporation. They were appointed directly to Class I and Class II on or after 1st September, 1956. The Corporation had fixed the age of retirement in its service book. The appellants were not paid salary for the period from January 1, 1965 to March 31, 1966. On a representation made by them, the Government of India issued an order dated June 30, 1967 directing that the employees who joined the service of the corporation on or before 1st October, 1956 shall retire on completion of 58 years of age and at any time thereafter on giving three months ' notice or salary in lieu thereof. The appellant No. 1 was appointed directly as a Class III employee by virtue of the settlement and the amendment of the regulations. The employees who were appointed to Class II and Class IV irrespective of the fact whether they were transferred employees or employees appointed after 1 st September,1956 were entitled to continue in service till 60 years of their age subject to the usual clause relating to premature retirement. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated July 30, 1966 passed by the Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants had not been paid salary from January 31, 1965 onwards and that they were entitled for payment of salary for that period. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that clause (b) of section 49(2) of the Act was not in terms applicable to the transferred employees who became the employees of Class III and Class I or Class II, as the case may be. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court erred in striking down regulation 19(2). [776F] 2.1 It is only in 1965 under the settlement that the age was raised to 60 years on their being promoted to a Class I post or Class III post. [778G] 3.1 In 1965 under section 11 of the , the age limit for retirement of employees who had joined the services of the Corpo ration belonging to Class III or Class IV would be 58 years. The appointing authority may at its discretion extend his service for one year at a time upto 60 years, but the competent authority may, if it is of the opinion that it is in the interest of theCorporation to do so, direct such employee to retire on attaining the age o superannuation or at any stage thereafter on give him three months' notice or wages in lieu of notice or pay in lieu thereto. [77G] 4.2 The High Curt erred in upholding the validity and sustainability of the impugned order dated January 31., 1966 passed under section 49 (2) by the State Government. [773A B] 5.1 Section 49(3) of The Act was enacted to provide for the benefit of employees belonging to class I or class II categories appointed to the service on or After 1st August, 1956 and in respect of whom the Corporation has fixed the ages of retirement as 58 years which corre sponds to the age Of superannuation in almost all the public sector establishments, the Central Government services and the State Governments services. [777A B C] 5 2.3 The High Courts erred in holding that clause(b) was not applicable to those transferred employees whose appointment had joined service after 1St September, 1966 by virtue o the settlement. [779D F] 4 3.4 In 1965 the age fixed for retirement in Class III was raised from 60 years to 58 years only because he had been promoted to Class IV only till he attained the ageof 60 years as a class III employee. The provisions of section 11 were not applicable in the transferred employee who joined service before 1 st August, 1966 and who joined services after 1th September, 1957 by virtue Of the settlement dated June 19, 1965.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India, the Chief Minister of Haryana and the Chief Justice of Punjab High Court. The Chief Justice sent a letter on 20 February 1975 to the Prime Minister, Chief Minister, Haryana and Haryana High Court for being handed over to him for his personal attention. The appellants did not take any action against them. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the contempt proceedings were dropped. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the letters were addressed by the deponent to the Chief Secretary, Haryana, and the Prime Ministers had no jurisdiction to take action against the persons who would criticise the Judge 's speech. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The letter in question did not constitute contempt of court. It was a mere communication addressed by one member of the Bar Association to another member of that association. [243E] 2. The contents of the letter were unchallenged and we are of opinion that the High Curt proceeded on the basis that there was no intention whatsoever on his part to scandalise the Hon 'ble Judge or this Hon ' ble Court or to lower the authority or undermine the prestige of the learned Judge or of the Hon'ble Court. [244E] 3. The letters in question were addressed to the District Bar Association, Bhiwani and were addressed at Charkhi Dadri. It is an article of faith with the deponent himself. Therefore, the deponent tender his apology to this Hon' ble Court for the same and prays for its acceptance. The deponent most respectfully submits that there is to be a finding of committal of contempt. [245G] 4. If in view of this Honble Court, the action of the deponent in addressing the letter in questions constituted for any reason contempt of Court, one would be more sorry than the deponent itself. Therefore the deponent tendered his apology. The affidavit in question does not constitute a contempt. It cannot be said that there has been any intention whatsoever by the appellants to scandalize the Hon.'ble Court or that the Judges concerned did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the court would take any step against the person who would criticize the Judge. [246E] 5. The contempt proceedings are dropped.

The petitioner was a registered dealer under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer held that certain sections of the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, were void from the date of commencement of the Constitution by reason of article 14 of the constitution and that the provisions of section 5(1) of the said Act were unconstitutional. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of sub section (4) of section 6 of the Act on the ground that certain provisions of the Indian Incometax Act, had become void from its date of the commencement of Constitution by virtue of article 19(1)(f) and that it was not competent to the Commission to make a report to the Central Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that sub section(4) did not confer any larger power on the Commission under the provisions Of the Indian income tax Act and that in any case the procedure prescribed by the Indian law was a good substitute for that prescribed by section 34 of the Income tax (Investigating Commission)Act, 1947. The appellant contended that the impugned Act violated article 14 inasmuch as it did not provide for an enquiry into the validity or otherwise of sub sections (1), (2), (3), (7) and (8) of Section 5 of the impugned act and that therefore the provisions contained in section 5 were void. Held, that the procedure to be followed by the Commission was a valid one and that there was no substantial difference between the two procedures. The procedure prescribed under section 34 was a fair substitute for the procedure laid down in section 7 which provides that subject to the provisions o sub section 4 of section 8 the Commission shall have power to regulate its own procedure and that procedure prescribed in section 34 is a good substituting for that provided by the Act. The provisions of sub clauses (3) of article 20 were not intended to be exhaustive or exhaustive but they were intended to operate only to the detriment of those dealt with under sub section 2(1). The procedure laid in section 8 was a complete code and did not offend any provision of law. The purpose of enacting sub section 3 of section 34 had been to ensure that the Commission could make an enquiry to ascertain whether there was substantial difference in the procedure for conducting investigation into escaped income or evaded income. The object of the legislation was to prevent evasion of tax on income both under section 5 and the procedure which prescribed by it. It was not intended that the provision contained in sub section should be so construed as to make it a part of the statute itself. The language used in section 4(4)(a) of Act, therefore, clearly showed that there could be no difference between those dealt under sub sections 2 and 3. The words "any person other than the person whose case or points in whose case is being investigated to rebut any evidence brought on the record against him" were intended only to cover cases where the investigation into an escaped income was limited to a maximum period of eight years, while under the Act it was open to the Government to make such enquiry as may be specified in that behalf. The section does not say that there is in this matter in the first stages some similarity in the procedures prescribed by sub sections 1, (2) and 3 which would operate to the prejudice of those persons dealt with thereunder. It only provides that for the purpose of enabling the person who whose case was or are being investigated, he shall on application made in this behalf and on payment of such fees as may been prescribed by rules, be furnished with certified copies of documents, statements, papers and materials brought on record by the commission.

The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, New Delhi (Respondent 1) was a "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act. The Federation failed to comply with the direction and contended that it was not an "establishment" as defined in section 2 (9) of The Act. Allowing the appeal, HELD: The definition of ' commercial establishment' in section2(j) of Act is far wider than that of "commercial Establishment". [356G] In the instant case, it is immaterial whether its activities bring its premises within the ambit of a "shop" or a " commercial establishment" because by the Memorandum of Association, Articles of Association and other material, it was held that these activities of the Federation carried on in the premises were also applicable solely to the promotion of the above objects and no part thereof could be paid as dividend or otherwise to any member. [356H] The definition given in section 3(5)(a) of 'commercial establishment' is far narrower than that contained in section 1(3) of . The mere word "trade" does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. It will bear repetition that the activity of the Association carried on by it amounts to a trade or business. [355A] In view of the fact that the definition of " commercial Establishment" in section (2)(j) is far more wider than the definition given therein, it cannot by any stretch of reasoning, be called a 'trade". [355C] The mere expression "commercial establishments" does neither mean something to which a profits is made nor is it distributed among its members. It would bear repetition if the activity carried on is a business or trade. Therefore, the definition in section 5(a) is wide enough to include the idea of profit, yet the definition gives the meaning to that expression. [354D] The fact of the matter is that the Respondent is a Federation of Federations and not an association of individuals traders, industrialists or businessmen. It is immaterial that before the High Court, it had been urged on behalf of the Appellants that before this Court, at no stage, it Was urged on the behalf of them that before it was urged on their behalf that before 'the High Court at no point, it could be contended that the activities carried on were a business. It was also not argued that because the definition refers to "some particular business or Trade" it is irrelevant whether its activity amounts to trade or profession.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who is a descendant of one Sri Babu Ausan Singh. The Income tax Officer held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income for "although the pension was determined with respect to the quantum of rent collection or the land could not be said to be the immediate source of the pension. He further observed that "in view of the objection of the appellant, the source of income is the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and, therefore, it is difficult to hold that the receipt of the respondent was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Income tax Act." The Appellate Tribunal held that the right which was conferred by the letter dated July 7, 1837, was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the income arose from a statutory obligation of the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate sources of the income were not land or rent collections from land, it was liable to tax under the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939. HELD: The right which is conferred by a letter and this conduct of the parties can only lead to the inference that by this settlement contained in the letter of July 7 1837 the right of the claimant 's predecessor in 1838 was created a right which could be said not to be an immediate source or source of his income but rests in the covenant in the deed to receive and appropriate to himself the income of his trust. [912 E] The right conferred by this letter is merely a measure, and indicated the source from which the allowance was given. Shah, J., speaking for the Court, observed: "The source of Income is clearly the arrangement arrive at in1837 and that is so notwithstanding that computation of remuneration is made as a percentage of the land revenue." [913 F] The income of a trust appropriated by the appellant as his remuneration is not received by him as rent or revenue of land; the character of the receipt is also derived from lands used for agricultural purposes.
