The appellant State Transport Undertaking, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of section 47(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 (for short 'the Act') on the ground that it violated article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the proviso to section 63(7) did not offend article 14 and was therefore void. On appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High court were wrong in distinguishing the decision of this Court in Sher Singh 's case and that the fourth sub clause of the proviso did not infringe article 14. [1015 E] 2. Section 47(2) does not say for example, for example like section 68 F(1), that the permit shall be granted to the State Transport undertaking by the State transport Undertaking in a case where the said area or route lies in more than one region and the Regional Transport Authority in any other case. 1015 The general scheme of the Act in the matter of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the case of a notified route or notified area, where under section 68F(1)(i) the permit has to be necessarily granted to a State Transport Undertakings by the Central Government in a Case where the same area or notified route lies In more than two regions and the regional Transport Authority, in any case. the claims of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. [1005 E F] 3. The proviso to sec. 63(1). does not mean that the State Government should have preference in the matters of stage carriage permit. It only means that in the cases of inter State routes, the claims for permits from the Indian Tourism Development Corporation and the State Tourist Department were substantially equal. The preference provided for by clause (iv) is unconstitutional and invalid. [1075 E F G] 4. Section 68F does not apply with equal force to the preference provided under section 47 (1). [1006 D] 5. The word 'preference ' occurring in section 47 of the , cannot be read as a restrictive expression or restricted meaning. It is only when the State has failed to consider the merits of the claims, that the proper course for us is to set aside the orders of the State and the Transport Appellate Tribunals and theHigh Court should direct the State authorities to re hear the appeals and dispose them of in accordance with law, after considering the claims and then considering the claim of the eligible applicants in the manner indicated in SherSingh 's cases and now. Clause (iv), of the Proviso to section63(7), does not indicate that for example section 68B applies with equal number to preference provided by the proviso thereto. [1106 E F; 1075 A B] 6. The expression 'prefer ' occurring In section 47 is wide enough to include operators of tourist cars or travel agents. It does not refer to any other kind of vehicle or transport agency. [1176 C D] 7. Section 57(7)(a) does no say, for instance, like section 63A. [1208 E F H] 8. The words 'prefers ' occurring therein are wide enough and include operators who do not get a certificate of approval from the Central or State Government because of the rule of preference contained in proviso to Section 63(07). [1076 D] 9. The second sub clause is unconstitutional, as it does not bear any such meaning. [1198 E] 10. The third sub clause does not mention that the application for stage carriage permits from a State transport undertaking for operating in any inter State route shall be given preference overall other applications. [121 G H] 11.

The respondent purchased a business in the name of M/s. Ram Reddy, who was a dealer liable to pay sales tax due from the dealer on the sale effected by him as defined in the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939 (Madras Act No. IX of 1939) and the amending Act has no application. The respondent contended that the State Government had power under section 19(1) and (2) of the Act to frame the impugned rule. Held, that the word 'assessment used in section 19 is beyond the rule making power of the State under sections 19(2)(c) and 19(3) of The Madras General sales Tax Act 1939 (Mad. IX Of 1939), which are ultra vires of the power of taxation conferred on the State by section 19 of the Madras Act IX of 1948, and that the tax assessed under this Act shall be paid in such manner and in such instalments, if any, and within such time as may be specified in the notice of assessment, not being less than fifteen days from the date of service of the notice. The word 'assess ' used in Section 19(4) is beyond what it was published in the Bombay Gazette on October 8, 1956, and the amended Act has therefore no application.. The word "assessment" used in s. 19(5) is not defined in section 2(1). It is a well settled principle of law that an order made under section 18 is intra vires of a statute and it cannot be utilised to enlarge the scope of section 10 regarding recovery and payment of tax from some other person under the Act. The words "assessment " used in sections 19 and 20 are wide enough to include the power to recover tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. The expression 'assessment ' used for the purpose of assessment is not intended to refer to an order passed by the authority concerned under section 17(1)(c). It has been held that the words "assessable under this section do not include the powers of recovering tax assessed by the assessing officer under section 16 of the, Act. [682 H; 603 A B] The word `assessment ' in section 20 is wide enough and it includes the power conferred on an authority to make rules to carry out the purposes of the. Act. It has no reference to an assessment made under the Madras Sales Tax (3rd amendment) Act, 1956. The definition of "assessment ' given in section 3(1), therefore, does not include a power conferred by section 18 of the Bombay General Sales tax Act, 1948.

The plaintiff was a public servant and was employed in the State of Gujarat. He was dismissed from service on February 2/4, 1955. The plaintiff filed a suit for a declaration that the order of dismissal dated February 2, 1955, passed by the Inspector General of Prisons, Saurashtra, was illegal and void on the ground that it contravened the provisions of article 311(2) of the Constitution. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there had been a breach of contract by the competent authority to provide a copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer before him and the tentative conclusions arrived at by the Enquiry officer were bound to influence him, and in depriving the plaintiff of a copy thereof he was handicapped. HELD: (1) The words "actionable wrong other than breach of contracts" in this context are wide words and include something more than torts, but even so where a suit is brought by a Government servant for arrears of salary, the decree more properly falls under section 60(2)(a). [179 G] (ii) Where, before the appointed day, the State Of Bombay is subject to any liability in respect of any actionable wrong other then breach of Contract, that liability shall, (a) if the cause of action arose wholly within the territories which, as from that day, are the territories of the State, be a liability of that State; and (b) in any other case, of the state of Maharashtra, but subject to such financial adjustment as may be agreed upon between the States of Maharashtra and Gujarat or, in default of such agreement, as the Central Government may by order direct. Where, immediately before the appointment day,the State of Bombay is not subject to a liability in regard to any actionable right other than a breach in contract, that liabilities shall, to the extent to which they would have been rights or liabilities of the Union of India, be rights or obligations of the Government of Maharashtra but subject only to such Financial adjustment as might accrue, under any such contract, as may agreed upon. Where immediately before appointed day the State Government of Bombay has made any contract in the exercise of its executive power for any purposes of the States, that obligation shall, unless the cause is shown by the plaintiff, be deemed to have been made in the exercising of the executive power, (iii) where a claim is brought forward by a discharge civil servant for the period that he was actually in office, the suit more properly falling under section 61. [179 E F] (iv) Where before the date appointed day i.e., the appointed date, the Government has made an agreement in the course of his executive power to determine the liability arising out of a contract, and the liability for payment of arrears of pay is the liability of the Central government but subject thereto such financial adjustments as may have accrued, under the contract shall, be recoverable by the State.

The plaintiffs ' land lies immediately to the south of the defendants ' land. The plaintiffs alleged that the respondents had encroached upon their coal mines on the southern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. The appellants contended that the suit was not barred by limitation, because they were bound to keep a barrier of 25 feet to the north of the defendant 's working and, therefore, the boundary could more satisfactorily and definitely be fixed with reference to the plans annexed to the subsequent lease deeds executed in favour of the successors in interest of the appellant and the respondents. The trial court held that the defendants had knowledge of the sinking of the quarries and pits in the encroached land. Held, that the plaintiffs were bound by the tenor of the article in the Limitation Act and also to the rules of evidence. The High Court accepted the finding of fact arrived at by the courts below on the assumption that the initial burden was on the respondents to prove that they had knowledge about the existence of the said encroachment only within three years thereof. In other words, the onus of proof to establish knowledge on the part of the respondents beyond the prescribed time was on them to prove the possession of the converted property and that is all. The defendants did not deny the fact that the entire burden was upon the defendants. They did not admit the fact in their written statement that they came to know of the removal of coal by the appellant or their possession of their coal removed beyond three years of the date of filing of the suit. In the absence of any acceptable evidence on their part, the High Court could not have accepted the findings of the courts that the earlier burden was discharged by them within three months of the filing of their written statements.

The appellant was a crosscutter. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. On June 25, 1958 Sankaran was informed that the proposed inquiry, if conducted, would lead to further friction and deterioration in the rank and file of the employees in general and also that maintenance of discipline in the undertaking would be prejudiced if he was retained in service. The appellant thereupon terminated the services of Sankaran under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental inquiry and the order was communicated to Sankaran the same day. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the action taken under r 18 (a) is mala fide and was not colourable exercise of the power given under r, 18(b). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The employer could defend the action under r., 18(c) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action took under r section 18 (c) is bona fide and is not colourable. [18C D] 2.1 The employer can defend the actions under r,. 18(d) by adducing evidence before it to show whether there was any misconduct or unfair labour practice. If the inquiry was not held by the employer and action was taken under that rule, there was nothing more to be said and that the employer could contest the action on behalf either of the employee or his representative. [19D] 2:2 The employer would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. [20E] 3.3 In a case where the employer wanted to take action for misconduct actually charged might be done away with. [21F] 4.4 The employer wanted that an inquiry should be held for misconduct, notice for which had been given to the employee and for which a departmental inquiry was intended to be held. If it is satisfied that the actions taken under such a rule were a colourable exercise thereof, it would have the jurisdiction to interfere and setaside such termination.[22G] 5.4 In this case the employer did not satisfy the tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication that there had been in fact in misconduct and hence the action was bona fide. [22F] 6.5 The employer was empowered to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action taken was under rs. 18 (d) of Standing Orders. [23C D].

The appellant, a tenant of a building in the Court of Small Causes at Ahmedabad, filed a suit against respondents 5 and 6 for a declaration that it was entitled to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. The Trial Judge held that the consent decree had not decided that the transaction between the parties of the year 1954 was in the nature of a lease; that the agreement dated December 1, 1960, created a lease and that the document dated November 27, 1954, created an lease and the consent order operated as res judicata. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the consent terms decree had no binding force and (ii) the document executed by the parties in favour of respondents 5 & 6 were not a lease ? Dismissing the appeal, HELD : 1.1 The question whether in law the jurisdiction of the Court is derived from section 28 of the Bombay Rent Control Act is derived out of section 28. [12B C] 1.2 The consent decree operated as a res judicata and that it related to a matter to be decided by the Court. [13C D] 1:3. The question then arises for consideration is whether in view of the consent judgment of this Court, the trial court had decided that question and allowed the whole question, that was closed once for all by consent decree. [14D E] 1 :4. In the instant case it was not decided whether the legal relationship arising out of the agreement between the respondents 5 to 6 was in fact barred by res judicata or estoppel under the provisions of section 92 of the Evidence Act. [15E F] 1.:5. The only thing that can be said is that so far as the agreement of November 27 1954, creating a lease, the Court has no jurisdiction on principles of res judicata to go into that question or to decide that question over again to the extent to which the Court, viz., the trial Court in the instant suit, proposed to go to that question. [16E] 1.(a) The only way that can legitimately be said to be that so long as the consent is not decided by a court it must be held that it relates to a case decided within the meaning of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [17G H] 2.1 In the present case, the question whether the consent was of the nature or of a tenancy or other character had to be determined in accordance with law. The High Court has recorded a finding that the relationship arising from the agreement was not in the character of a Lease and concluded "It is not open to me in revision at this stage to express any opinion about the rights and contentions of the parties with reference to the agreement. [18G H; 19A] 2:2 The only question that can arise for consideration whether in fact the subordinate Court has decided the question of resjudicata, or whether it has decided that issue. [19B C D] 3.1 There is no doubt that the jurisdiction and power of the court to decide a question finally concluded by consent is derived under section 28(2) of the Act but at the same time if an issue is in fact brought before it by way of appeal or in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, then the Court may have decided that questions over again by consent. [20G H]. 3.2 In the view of this finding the question must be answered in the affirmative and not in favour. [22B C E] 4.3 The only matter that can possibly be said about the agreement is whether it related merely to a matters to be adjudicated by the court.

The respondent was appointed as a Pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was working as a pilot Officer. In the year 1972 he was declared unfit by a Medical Board and was, therefore, inval idated from I.A.F. The Government of India issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The State of Uttar Pradesh adopted the same scheme. The respondent filed a Writ Petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order of termination on the ground that he had been wrongly appointed as Pilot Ad hoc Commission in the year 1973 and not beyond that date unless there was a further extension. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the interim order granted by the High court could not be sustained and the Writ petition was liable to be dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State of U.P., that the respondent had been rightly appointed as pilot Adhoc Commission in 1973 and therefore, he should be reinstated in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period of his appointment beyond 30th August, 1985. Dismissing the Appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court has not committed any error in holding that there was no order of extension of service to the respondent. [243E] 2.2 The interim order dated 10.7.1986 passed by the Governor on review and restore the Judgment dated 24.3.1988 passed in the Writ Petitions is liable to set aside. [244F] 3.1 In the circumstances, the High Curt has rightly held that the termination order could not have the effect of controlling the jurisdiction of the High Courts to dispose of the Writ petitions on merits as it did on 24.03.1988. [245G] 4.2 It is open for the opposite parties to con tinue till he completed the age of 58 years. If the respondent succeeds in his Petition it would be made available forthwith to the petitioner by way of an appointment.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted the accused but maintained his conviction under section 304 Part I, IPC. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court should not interfere with the order of acquittal merely because another view is possible. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court was well justified in rejecting the evidence of P. 1 to 3 and that the discrepancies noticed by the learned Sessions Judge were of a minor character and that they have been unduly magnified by the leaned Sessions Judge. [723 E] (2) The discrepancies noticed in the evidence are of a major nature, which can be dismissed with the sentence 'of course it is possible but not in the least probable' the case is proved beyond reasonable doubt, but nothing short of that will suffice. [824 C] (3) The accused must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. If the evidence is so strong against a man as to leave only a remote possibility in his favour, which cannot be dismissed without the sentence "of course" it is impossible but not possible for the High court to interfere with such order merely because some other view is also possible. [924 D] (4) The prosecution tried to make P. W. 1 and the accused was content with a bare denial but in the Court of Sessions he stated that they had been unduly put up by the repeated refusal of his brother and father, the neighbourers P.W. 1. It is obvious that he must have beardised by the constant refusal of her brother and that when two views are possible, the accused must be reasonable.

The appellant was a Judge of the High Court. He was appointed as a Judge in the year 1952. On his appointment he was transferred to the High court. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Curt, contending that the sanction under Section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 is not necessary for prosecution of a person holding such an office and that the same can be taken only if it is read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which the disproportion and his inability to satisfactorily account can be inferred. The High Court dismissed the writ petition, but on appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The power to punish a Judge or Chief Justice of India is not a vertical superior of any other person, nor can it apply to the Judges of the Supreme Court and for that matter even to the Supreme court Judges. [620B] 1.2 The words in clause (e) have to be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of the competent authority under Section6(1)(c) of the Act and this can be done only if the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office. [720C] 1:3 The words "any other person" in clause(e) are clear pointer in the direction that the Parliament has not as yet considered it expedient to enact any such law for the trial and punishment on the charge of corruption of a superior Judge instead of the general law. [821B] 2.4 The words used in clause 5(e), have to take their colour from the scheme of which the Public servant is sought to be inferred, and not to the Chief Justice or the ChiefJustice exercising only moral authority over his colleagues in the Supreme Courts and the High Courts, much less the Supreme Curt Judges: The incumbent of the office of Chief Justice, exercising only administrative power over his subordinates in the manner provided in Article 124(5) as the only punishment; and a special law enacted by the Parliament under Article 124 (5), even for investigation and proof of any misbehaviour alleged against a superior judge instead of general law was clearly visualised when the alleged misbehavior is connected to his office, [721C] 2:5. The words 'any other persons' in clause 4(1) (c) have been given some significance which would include the Chief Justices and Judges, who are not members of that House, much higher than the Supreme Judge or the High curt Judges. It is for this reason that the Legislature has not made any provision which cannot apply to a Judge holding such office. The fact that the legislature did not enact any other law even then for the investigation into allegations of corruption against a subordinate Judge and for his trial and punishments for that offence and rest content merely with enacting the , to provide for the procedure for remov al of a Judge under Article124(4) is a clear pointer to the direction, that the President of India may be deemed to be the authority to grant sanction in accordance with the procedure envisaged in Article124 (5) read with Article 2 18. [758G] 3:6 The words of clause (ee) have not been given any meaning which could possibly apply to Judges of High Court Judges, since the Chief Judge of India exercises only moral power over their colleagues in a Supreme Court or theHigh Court Judges. The mere fact that a Parliament did not provide for any special law would not make out any prima facie Case for obtaining sanctions under Section 5(1).

The appellant was a member of the Saha caste and not a member. The respondent filed an election petition under section 100(1)(c) of the Representation of People Act, 1951 against the appellant for the declaration that he belonged to a Scheduled Caste specified in item 40 of the Schedule Castes. The appellant contended that the appellant belonged to an independent caste which had nothing to do with Sunri caste and that it was not open to him at the trial to contend as he was excluded from the Scheduled Caste category because he belonged only to a smaller caste group within the larger caste group of Sunris, distinguished himself by their surname. The Election Tribunal held that the Sahas were originally a smaller castes and were for that reason not a mere sub caste strictly so called within the Sunri tribe. It further held that as the appellant bore the surname Sahas, he did not belong to the Scheduled Castes specified in items 40 and 40 of item 40. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent had established that the appellants belonged to the Saha Caste and that therefore did not, therefore, belong to that caste. Held, further, that the High Court was right in holding that the finding of the Election Tribunal that the respondents were members of the Scheduled Tribe specified in Item 40 was correct. The word 'Saha ' in the item must, without more, refer to a caste group which formed the smaller caste groups within the bigger caste group called Sahas. The appellant was a tenant of the premises in question. The appellant, who maintained that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the workmen to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The Industrial Tribunal also rejected the contention of the appellant that the increased wage scale had necessarily been mentioned in the award and that there was no mention of giving any ad hoc increase in the basic pay of individual workman. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The word "flat" is not defined in the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. There can be no doubt that a workman who has been employed for wages on the date of his appointment and who has not been paid, is entitled to get the additional pay if he is not paid. But when there is a dispute between the parties regarding payment of any amount due to him, it would be more concerned with the immediate benefits according to them That was why the Industrial Tribunal thought that an all round flat increase to the pay of each individual workman was intended to each of the employees in the category of Draftsmen and Rs 100/. [502F] 5. There could be no dispute about the fact that there is no mention in the order that all employees were entitled to receive additional pay. The omission of the words to each employee first after the figure Rs. 50/ and thereafter after the figures Rs 150/- and Rs 150/-, would result in serious anomalous situation. [403F] 6. There has been a clear statement of its intention is found in paragraph 22 of the Award where the Tribunal stated that all workmen were to be fitted into the revised scales of pay, dearness allowance and there was also no mention about giving any Ad hoc increase of salary to each individual workmen.

The appellant was employed as a driver of a truck carrying goods. The appellant appealed to this Court on the question whether the refusal to pay wages at rates fixed by an award could be treated as wages under section 2 of the said Act. HELD: 1.1 The words "any remuneration payable under an award" in section 2 are wide enough to include wages directed to be paid by industrial adjudication and that they must be terms which arise out of the contract between the employer and the employees. [419B] 1.2 The words used in section 15(1) are wide and comprehensive. They must be given their ordinary meaning, unless there is something in the context or in the scheme of the agreement to indicate that the intention was to make new contracts between employers and workmen. If they were not express, it would have been open to the authority under the Act to decide whether the wages prescribed by an order could be regarded as wages within section 2. [519C] 1:3 The words in question need not be express and can be implied; but they must also be terms of which arise from the contract of employment, either express or implied. But they must have been terms which arises out of industrial adjudication. If it is shown to the satisfaction of Industrial adjudication that the very purpose for which industrial adjudication has been given the peculiar authority and right of making new contracts would continue to govern the relations between the employers and the workmen till it was replaced by other contract, it can and often enough it do radically change the terms of the Contract of employment. [619D] 1.:4 The very purpose of which industrial adjudic has been conferred the peculiar Authority and right to make fresh contracts between the employees and the employer may elapse in respect of both of which special provisions have been made under sections 23 and 29 respectively the new contract would continue, if a change or revision of the terms appears to be justified, it could, and often sufficient it does radically changed the terms Of the contract employment. The words employed in section 14(1)(vi) are comprehensive enough to cover wages directed by an industrial tribunal. [719E] 1 :5. The very object for which Industrial adjudication has already been given is that on references made under section 10(1), it must be shown that they constitute part of the term ' wage' either express, or implied, were fulfilled, be payable. [819F] 2.6 The words 'any remuneration paid by an employer to a workman under any contract of service, express or expressed, are comprehensive and comprehensive enough. They should be terms and which arise in out of employment and the period for which it remains binding on the parties may elapce in respect Of both of them till it has been replaced by others. The word 'wages' is not defined in section 3(vi). [820F] 1.?7 The words are wide to include remuneration directed to pay by industrial adjudic, but they should be words which ariseout of the contracts between employer and workmen made under the provisions of sections 23 & 29 respectively. [820C D] 2:8.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. On the date of the incident, he was posted as Sub Divisional Magistrate in the District of Patiala. The Company challenged the validity of an agreement entered into between the Company and its employees at Calcutta under which the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age Of 55. The Tribunal held that in all the awards in recent times there was no uniform trend in Bombay region to fix the retirement age at 60, that is, between 1952 and 1961, that the trend in the Bombay region had been to fix retirement age of clerical and subordinate staff at 60 years subject only to the employee passing a Medical examination on reaches the age o 55. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the workmen that the decision of the Tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem was erroneous, because it was not correct to say that the error committed by the Tribunal was in fact inaccurate and was therefore liable to be set aside. HELD: The Tribunal had found that in Bombay the trend had been about fixing the retirement ages at 60 and that its present conclusion that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court in appeal, was on the whole unsound. [446B] In all the cases the age was fixed at 60. On a consideration of all the facts and circumstances disclosed by the oral and documentary evidence on this record, we are satisfied that the Tribunal had not committed any error in fixing the age for retirement at 60; and that it was rightly held that the conclusion recorded by this court in some of its earlier decisions as to the relevant trend in this case was erroneous. [546C] The Tribunal has failed to notice that in the Calcutta region there is a general agreement with regard to the age and retirement of the workmen 's case that the recent trend in Madras region had not been to fixing the superannuation age at 58 subject to certain exceptions which had been introduced by agreement for the Bombay employees retirement at the ageof 55. [646B C] The very few departures from this practice which the Tribunal has mentioned are, in our opinion, wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend. What the Tribunal have failed to notices is that instances which may justify a revision of the judicial opinion expressed on an previous occasion about a particular trend must be strong and unambiguous and they must speak for the period both before and more particularly after the previous finding had been recorded in the matter. 429 The very many departuresfrom this practice, which the tribunal has mentioned were, in my opinion, totally insufficient to show any slowness down of that trend must have been strong and categorical and they should speak forthe period bothbefore and more especially after the earlier finding hadbeen recorded in its matter. 430 The Tribunal was therefore justified in interfering with the award fixing the date of retirement at 58 years.

The appellants were the partners of M/s Barium Chemicals Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as 'the Company') and the Company was formed for the purpose of manufacturing and selling of various products. The workmen were drawing basic pay at a particular stage in the time scale of the Sastry award as modified by the Desai award. The bank had to pay the minimum of the scales provided under the Sastry Award. The workmen filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Desai Award on the ground that it was not in accordance with the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and that the Desai Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the reference. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Sastry Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide the question as to whether the workmen would be fitted in the new scales of pay from January 1, 1959 on stage to stage adjustment basis, i.e., workmen who were drawing Basic pay at the particular stage and were drawing higher basic pay under the Desai awards as modified would draw basic pay in the scale then in force in the bank concerned. The appellants contended that the High court had jurisdiction under article 226 of the Constitution to decide questions of fact relating to the interpretation of paragraph 5.356 of the National Industrial Tribunal (Bank Disputes) Award, and that it could not entertain a writ application on the basis of the decision of this Court in [The National Industrial Disputes Tribunal vs The Workmen] ; , followed. Held: (i) The High court was right in holding that no question of law arose out of the award. It was not competent to decide any question of fact which would arise out of a writ proceeding. The jurisdiction of the High courts under article 227 is limited to the determination of questions of facts and if it is found that there has been some error or mistake apparent on the face of the record, it can interfere with such findings. (ii)The High Court was not right in interfering with the finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal. The power of the court under article 136 is limited only to the question whether a particular question of facts is involved in the case and if so what should be the position. If there has, been some mistake or error apparent on record, the High 'Court can interfere only when it comes to the conclusion that the findings are perverse or based on no evidence or where the finding is perverse or suffers from patent illegality or irregularity. The powers of the Court under article 32 and 226 are wide enough to cover all cases where there has not been any miscarriage of justice or where a manifest error or an error apparent in the face thereof, or where two views are possible on the evidence adduced by the parties, one view is that the jurisdiction of a court to decide disputes between the parties should be exercised only if it comes within the parameters of section 22(1)(f) and not when there has no jurisdiction. The Court can interfere even if there has had been some miscarriage of procedure or where there have been an error of law apparent on its face, or when two views have been possible on any evidence which could be said to be erroneous or perverse. Where the High Courts are satisfied that a question of jurisdiction is involved and it has been shown that there was no error apparent or patent in the appreciation of evidence or the findings recorded by them suffer from patent errors, the Court can refuse to exercise its powers under article136 of the constitution. (iii)The power of this court under Article 136 is wide enough and is not limited only in cases where it has jurisdiction to interfere with an order of acquittal passed by a court of competent jurisdiction or where an error is apparent on face of record, but also when there have had been an erroneous appreciation of the evidence or when the findings of fact are perverse.

The appellants, who were the owners of four acres of land in Calcutta, applied for a lease of the Begumbari land to the respondent No. 1 on February 12, 1981. The respondent No, 1 was granted a lease by the Government of West Bengal on February 13, 1981 and the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 were granted a licence for the construction of Five Star Hotel. On March 12,1981, the respondent no. 1 filed an application before the State Government under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') seeking permission to sell the Begambari land in question. The State Government rejected the application on the ground that the lease was not a licence and that the respondent had no locus standi to file the application. On appeal by the appellants, the Division Bench held that the decision taken was neither unreasonable nor arbitrary and that taking away of four acre of land from the Zoo for the purpose of encouraging setting up industries within the State, the Government was quite alive to the need for expan sion of the zoo for a single day without the essential services which were being provided in the four acres o f land proposed to be given for the hotel. The appellants filed an appeal before this Court against the decision of the Division bench. The question whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal right ly held that on the findings and in law the Tribunal had jurisdiction ly to answer the question referred to it, the High court was in wrong answering the questions in the affirmative. Section10 did not come into play when the money was transferred by further entries in their own account books, it resulted in a valid transfer even the entries in those accounts and corresponding credits to the accounts of L and K. The amount gifted was only Rs.4,299 but the unuti lised overdraft of the firm was only RS.4.299. [134E] 6. Section 11 did not bring into existence any new gift on which the amount transferred could be included in its income tax net wealth. [135B] 7. The appellant was appointed as a district judge in March 1962, and he was posted as superintendent and legal remembrancer in March 1963. On October 10, 1966, the State Government sent back judicial officers working in administrative posts as district judges or as addl. district judges. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the High court holding that those officers had no authority to hold the posts in question and that the transfer ordered by the High was unsustainable. The High Court dismissed the writ petition, but on appeal by special leave, this Court held that the order passed by the State government transferring Shri B.K. Panda as superintendent was not a law secretary, deputy law secretary and superintendent, legal remywrancer and that it was within the powers of the Governor under article 235 as the control vested in him by article 235 is vested in the High Courts under article 236(b) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High 'Court was not justified in holding that the officers had a right to hold those posts for three years or more, and that as the post of superintendent and judicial remembrance and ex officio additional law secretary to the government of Orissa, the High "Court was within its powers under article 226 of the constitution. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High ' Court is not competent to exercise its power in posting Shri B,K. Bose as superintendent, and legal personis working in the secretariat. [623B] 1.2 The High Courts are vested with the control over the officers who preside over those courts. They have also been given the power to fill up any of the posts by transfer of judicial officers. [524C D] 1:3 The High court is competent to issue a writ of mandamus against the government as well as the concerned officers to implement the transfers ordered by them. [643E F] 2.1 In the instant case, the order was passed in consultation with the High Curt and by and large on the recommendation of the Chief Minister. Patro had not been placed at the disposal of the government for any definite period, it was open to the High Judge to recall them and post them as presiding officers of district courts. Hence, the question whether those officers have no authority or competence to hold these posts in the matter is not sustainable. [641G H] 2:2 The transfer of Shri B.,K. Das as superintendent of Legal rememb Offender and exofficio Additional law secretary was not an order passed under article 233 but it was made only in the context of the question that arose for decision. [651A D] 3.1 There is no provision in the Constitution which empowers the High to issue any writ of certiorari against the Government as well or the concerned officer to exercise control over them by transfer, promotion and posting. The power vested in a High Court under article 227 of the is not an absolute one but only a discretionary power. [661B] 3:2 In the present case, there was no provision for issuing any writ against the State as well. [671C D; 67A C] 4.3 There is nothing in the constitution which empowers it to issue such writs. The Constitution does not confer any right on a person who has been appointed or promoted and posted to the cadre of district judges, nor does it confer any power on him to act as law secretary or deputy law Secretary or deputy Law Secretary or Deputy Law Secretary.

The appellant, a co sharer, was the vendor of the respondent 's brother. The respondent ' s brother had purchased land from his father and mother in the year 1962. The sale deed was executed on 12th January, 1963. The appellant filed an application under section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Preemption Act, 1913 for pre emption of the appellant 's son 's sons 's daughters 's daughter 's sister 's brothers and brother 's father 's mother 's husband. The trial court held that there was no infringement of Article 19(1) (f) of Constitution. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court upheld the constitutional validity of clause 'fourthly ' and 'fifthly ' of section 15 of the Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression 'other co sharers ' in section 15 (1)(b) of Punjab Pre preemptionemption Act refers to only those co shars who do not fail under clause 'Fourthly ' or 'Secondly '. [515E] 2.2 In the instant case also the suit land belonged to more than one co sharter and had not been sold jointly by all the co sharters. The expression "other cosharers" in section 14(1A)(b), is meant to serve as a residuary clause to ensure 127 that, no co sharker is left out. [615B] 3.2 The legislature desired to confer the right of pre emation on specified family members of the vendor or vendors who were specified in the erstwhile first three clauses of section 14 (1A) and with a view to covering all the remaining co sharts not specifically mentioned the preceding clauses it used the expression 'Other co sharERS ' in the fourth clause which was meant to serving as a special clause to ensuring 127 that no cosharer is leftout. [715C] 3:3 The legislature wanted to confer a right of preemption on certain relatives or relatives of the vendors who are specified in those erstwhile first two clauses of Section 15(2)(b). It desired to give a benefit to those relative or relatives who were not specified in that clause. [815E H; 816A] 4.4 The legislature intended to confer an additional right on certain relative or relative of the purchaser or vendors, who are not specified therein. [917F] 5.5 In the context, it becomes clear that the legislature desired that no Co sharer is left to out. Hence, the object of clause "fourthly" in clause 'Thirdly ' in clause (b) was to deny the right to hold, acquire or dispose of property conferred by Article 19 (1)(f) and clause fourthly of section15(1). [816B] 6.6 The expression ''other cosharer' in clause "Fourthly" refers to all the members of a family who do either fail under clauses 'Second or 'Thirdally or 'Firstly or 'firstly or secondly ', respectively. [820C] 7.7 In the present case also, the suit property belonged to one cosharers and had no right of sale or dispose off the land or property sold or a part thereof. The question is whether the intention of the legislature was to confer such a right on the vendor. It is seen that the expression "any co shar er" in Section 14(2) (b), refers to both the cosharers who do neither fail under any of the clauses mentioned in the preceding clause and the father ' or vendors Fourthly, in the other co sharor and the tenants can exercise the right conferred on them by that provision.

The appellant was an Advocate of the High Court of Bombay. He had a standing of about thirty years. The grounds were not vague or not, but want of bona fides, as well as the non application of mind, on the part of the detaining authority, viz., the Government, which for this purpose must be taken to be different from the police. The High Court dismissed an application made by the appellant under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that the grounds furnished are vague and not in public interest. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the non communication of the decision to disclose facts considered against public interest cannot be said to have hampered his constitutional right of representation, and that the failure of the authority to communicate the decision is fatal to the detention order. Held: (i) The right of the detenue to be furnished particulars, at least to that extent, it will enable him to present to the Advisory Board his difficulties in making a proper representation and to convey to it a request for obtaining the requisite particulars from the State under section 10 of the Act for their own information and consideration. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non Communication of the order decision cannot be held to have adversely affected his constitutional rights of representation. The right to be supplied particulars, is subject to the limitation under article 22(6) whereby disclosure of facts considered to be against public interests cannot be implied in these circumstances. If the appellant bad exercised his right to ask for particulars at the time when the grounds were furnished, there can be no doubt that he would have been furnished then the very information which has been supplied in paragraph 12 of the Under Secretary 's affidavit and there is nothing to suggest that this question was not considered by the detaining Authority at the relevant time when it was made. The non communication, therefore, cannot be construed as having hampered the constitutional right to representation. [723C D] (ii)The right of a detenue to make a representation is subject only to the limitations under article 19(6), and not to any restriction on the exercise of the power by the authority concerned. The obligation to communicate cannot be inferred in these cases having regard to the nature of the 393 grounds on which the detention is based and the nature thereof, as was pointed out by this court in the State of Bombay vs Atma Ram Sridhar Vaidya(1) in the following passage: "The right to make representation is a constitutional right. The power not to disclose information considered against Public interest cannot therefore be implied In these circumstances, it can only mean that the right of an detenue to have access to the relevant material at the place where the detention was based and his personal knowledge or belief are likely to be affected by the prejudicial activities carried on by him." [724C D; 723A B] (iii)The non communication is not in a public interest to disclose the details of the activities alleged to have been carried on so as to nullify the constitutional rights. The question whether or not article 22 (6) of the constitution overrides the constitutional Right to be furnish particulars under article 21(6).

The respondent was a member of the Indian Army. He was dismissed from service by the General Court Martial on April 9, 1959. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the . Rule 14 provides that when after considering the reports on an officer 's misconduct, the Central Government is satisfied or the C in C shall communicate the view of the Central government or his views, as the case may be, to the officer together with all reports adverse to him and he shall be called upon to submit his explanation and defence. The Central Government dismissed the respondent from service. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of Constitution for a direction that r 14 of Army Rules 1954, be ultra vires and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that rs 14 of Defence Rules, 1955, were ultra vires. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that r 15 of the Defence Rules 1954 did not apply to a case where under, subject to the provisions of the Act and such rules, the C In the instant case, the respondent was not guilty of any misconduct. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : 1.1 The words "subject to the provision of this Act" occurring in section 19 of the read with r.14 of the Rules,1954, are not ultra vires but they merely refer to the rules and subject to other provisions of this act. [723D] 2.2 The words 'subject to any other provisions' occurring in s. 19 of The read with rule 14 of these Rules do not mean that there should be rules and so, the power conferred by sub section (1) of section 191 is not ultra Art. 14. [824E F] 3.3 The words used in section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, are "subject lo the provisions" of this. Rule 14 is such a rule : it is, therefore, not ultra Arts. 14 and 19 of Army Rule, 1954. [820G H; 823A] 4.4 The words "'subject to this Act " occurring in Section 19 of , are such a Rule ; they speak of removal of a person from the service. [824B C] 5.5 The words mentioned in section 191(2) (a) of the , are not intra vires the Constitution. They merely refer only to rules and regulations made thereunder. It is, however, open to the Central Govt to remove a person under section 19 or to remove from the Service any person whom it considers necessary so to do. [823D] 6.6 The words in section 192(2)(a) are not inter vires the Act. They refer only only to rule and regulations which may be made by the Central Gove rnment. It does not mean a rule where under subject to any provision of the law, the central Government has been given the power to remove an officer from the services. [822G] 7.7 The words are "Subject to the other provisions" in section 190(2). They refer to rules or regulations made under the Act, and such regulations, the general rule is that there must be a valid rule where the Central Govern ment has been conferred power to dismiss or remove from service any person either under section 18 or 19 of this Regulation. [825C] 8.8 The words of "subject" occurring therein are not beyond the scope of the authority conferred by section 190 (2)(b) of Army Act, 1954 and they refer only in respect of disciplinary matters.

The appellant company was assessed to octroi duty under r. 21 of the Rules framed by the State Government in exercise of its powers conferred on it by r. 22 of the rules framed under the Act. The appellant company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the levy and the order of the State imposing octroi duty on the ground that it was necessary for the Panchayat to have the octroi limits fixed with the approval of the Collector before levying octroi under r, 21. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Standing Committee inspected the premises of the Company but in their order they have given very scanty facts, They do not say whether the tea is crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. [223C D] 2.2 The Standing committee inspected the building and found that there was no evidence to show that the tea was crushed, processing or treated as a marketable product. The Standing Committees inspected the buildings of the company but in its order they had given very Scanty Facts, They did not say what the requirements were. [224F] 3.3 The Standing committees inspected the factory premises and found no evidence about the existence of any such tea. It was only when the Standing Committee visited the premises that it came to know that the Tea was crushed processed or converted into a saleable commodity, how could the tax be levied from the date specified in the notice. [225B] 4.4 The Standing Standing Committee did not follow the procedure contemplated by law in the matter of imposing octroi and the rate at which it is to be levied. It merely stated that if the tea had been crushed processed, processed and treated chemally to convert them into a marketed commodity, whether processed or subjected chemically, then how could it be levied? [225C] 5.5 The Standing Orders prescribing procedure for levying tax or fee are not confined to octroi duties only. [226B] 6.6 In the instant case, the Standing Committees visited the factory and found nothing material to show whether the Tea is crushed processed and processed chemically. They did neither say whether they were imported into octroi limits of the Panchayat for consumption, use or sale therein and at such rates as may be decided by it but also the rules relating to that tax which must mean the action taken under the act and rules. [222C] 7.7 The Standing orders prescribing procedure in r.3 and 4 are not restricted to octroi. They do no mention whether the Rules prescribe procedure for imposing tax or fees and are not applicable to octroi or fee. [232B] 8.8 In the result the appeal is allowed, and it is declared that the levy of octroi from April 1, 1963, in accordance with law was regularised. The case is remanded to the High court to deal with the question whether the Company brought tea into the octroi limit of the panchayat for consumption use or sell therein.

The appellant No. 1 was prosecuted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1)(b) of the , and was convicted by the Chief Presidency Magistrate, Bombay, and sentenced to a fine of Rs. 5 to a sum of Rs, 1 (now appellant No 1) and its Manager H. The appellants challenged their conviction before the High Court under section 32(1), read with sections 33(2)(b), 34(1). The High Court dismissed the appeal but confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that as the conciliation proceedings had continued for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952, further proceedings for conciliation were illegal and therefore the appellants could not be convicted under section31(1); (i) that the dismissal could not have been said to be one within the words " pendency of conciliation proceedings ". Held: (i)(a) The provisions of section 33 are mandatory in character and they cannot be construed as directory. It is true that section 12 contemplates the submission of the report by the Conciliation Officer within 14 days but that does not affect the pendency of the conciliation proceeding and if for some reason the Conciliation officer delays the submission or his action (1) ; No doubt section 12 envisages that the report should be made and the proceedings closed within a fortnight and if proceedings are not carried on, as they were in the present case, or if the Conciliation Officers do not make their report within 14 day he may be guilty of breach of duty but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an end after 14 days. The provisions Of section 12(6) of The Act clearly contemplate the submission by the conciliation officer within 14 months and if that report is received by the appropriate Government, the proceedings are closed. [723 C] (ii)The provisions of sections 33 and 34 are mandatory and they do not support this contention as the termination of the Conciliation proceedings is deemed to take place when the report under section 12 is made by the Board but only terminate as provided in section 20(2) (b). The provisions in section 12 are mandatory. They cannot be read as directory, and they can be construed so as to give effect to the intention of the legislature.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , hereinafter called the 'Act ' on the ground that he was falsely implicated and was not at all concerned with the murder. The District Magistrate, Dhanbad in respect of the said detenu made an order of detention against him under section3(2)(a) of . The petitioner/ appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of preventive detention. The High Court dismissed the writ petition and the appeal was allowed by the Division Bench. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the detenu that the order passed by the District Magistrate was invalid and on relevant considerations, the service of the detention order could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order was necessary for putting him back in jail. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The continued detention of the petitioner under the Act is not justified. [910B] 2. The service of order of Detention on the detenu while he was in custody and there is no indication that this factor or the question whether the said person might be released or that there was a possibility of his release, was taken into consideration by the detaining Authority properly and seriously before the service. [ 910C D] 3. The order of the District magistrate, Dhanbad, is set aside. If, however, the detenu is released on bail in the aforesaid criminal cases, the matter of service of that order would be reconsidered by the appropriate authority in accordance with law. There will, therefore, be no orders for release of the Petitioner/ appellant. [810E] 4. The petitioner was in jail and there was no real danger of his being released, the power of preventive bail should not be exercised. In these circumstances, the continued detention order of detenu under the act is not illegal and on irrelevant considerations, it cannot be justified. If a man is in custody, and there are indications that transfer of the prisoner from one prison to another was taken but at the time of service there was any real danger, of his releasing, the powers of preventive Detention should not have been exercised. [710G] 5. The detention order when it was passed was not invalid and therefore on relevant consideration, the services of the person might have been without consideration of all the aforesaid relevant factors, the petitioner could not have be put into preventive custody. [610B D] 6. If however, a man was in detention and there were no real likelihood of his having been released, then the power Of preventive detention should not ordinarily be exercised but it may be mentioned that in the instant case there was an apprehension that the detenu might be detained in jail for whatever reasons, therefore the order could be justified only against a particular person. [1010C] 7. The detaining authority had confirmed the order. There is no statement in the petition that the petitioner was on bail and there being any real threat of his detention or other factors which can justify the detention of a person might has been taken into account by the Detaining Authority properly. [1110D] 8. If that is the position, then however disreputable the antecedents of a man might have be without consideration considering all the relevant factors. The detenu could not be put in preventive custody because there was possibility of release, being released or even that there were any real likelihood about his release. [1210E D] 9. If the actual order of bail was served upon the petitioner, the detention would be justified if the order is passed on the aforesaid materials may be reconsidered in accordance to law. [1310G H; 1311A B] 10.

The appellant, a manufacturer, shroffs and dealers in gold trade, i.e., manufacturers, shoppers and dealers of gold was carrying on business as a money lender or banker on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business. The Administrator refused permission to carry on business on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been 954 provided by reference to which the power conferred upon him thereunder could be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. The High Court held that the impugned provision is violative of article 14 of the Constitution and consequently quashed the provisions of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the power of the administrator under the Act is not absolute in as much as the Administrator can authorise the third person to carryon business as money lender, banker or any other business in the premises of the dealer and while implementing such limited restrictions or granting relief against the same he will be guided by the policy and purpose of the enactment and by the prime consideration that circumvention of the other provisions of The Act shall not be premitted. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The scheme of the Gold Control as envisaged by the Act requires more than sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. It does not impose any blanket or 956 absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on any business as such dealer but he is prevented only from carrying out business as an money lender on the Security of any articles, ornaments or both unless authorised by the administrator so to do, banking or any others business in that premises in connection with which he carries on business are carried on. [112D F] 1.2 The scheme and the Scheme of the impugned Act requires sufficient guidance for the discretion conferred upon the Administrator while granting or renewing a license to a dealer. It is not necessary that there should be some guidelines or guide line having been 955 provided by the reference to whom the power conferral of a very wide and vague power upon the administrator should be exercised. [113E F] 2.1 In the instant case, the Administrator as is evident from this provision, is given unlimited authority or power to refuse permission or grant permission. The expression 'anticipated demand ' was really vague and incapable of assessment leading to a great deal of uncertainty; similarly the expression (1)AIR 1971 Patna, 240. 112. 112A. 27(6) on the grounds that it conferred a very limited wide and comprehensive power upon him under sec. 5(1)(a) of the the Act has to be upheld. [114G H] 2:2 The policy and the scheme affords sufficient guidance in the matters of exercising discretion under the section. The object is not to impose any arbitrary or uncanalised powers upon a person who carries on his business as the money lender but he was prevented only by from carrying business as cash lender or bankers on the securities of any other trade, ornamentation or both. Even the restriction in the case of a third person in carrying on trade as a dealer but who is prevented merely from carrying On business as goods lending, banking and any other commercial business in those premises in that particular area but he has been prevented only therefrom from carryingon business. [115G H; 116A B] 3:3 The policy or the scheme of section 28 does not cast any blanket power upon a licensee to carry out business on his security of articles, bullion or both if authorised by him. Even though there is no parity of situation or circumstances the doctrine of parity of reasoning cannot be invoked.

The appellants were the owners of agricultural lands situated in Eragudi village, Musiri taluk, Tiruchirappalli district. The properties belonged to the temple and they claimed that they had acquired title by adverse possession prior to 1 1 1929, but on the basis that it was beyond the authority of the manager, the lower appellate Court found that "it was evident that from the very beginning, Pachai Kandai Udayavar and his family had been claiming beneficial interest in the property and they were not holding the same as managers of the trust. The High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and held that "the transfer was effected by the manager as manager purporting to deal with the property as belonging to the religious endowment." In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the question as to whether a transfer effected by an order of the Manager in regard to properties belonging to a religious endowment is void ab initio, and that if the title of the alienees in regard thereto had been acquired by adverse Possession prior to the date of the transfer, it would not be affected by the provisions of article 134 B. Held, further, that the High Court was in error in reversing the decisions of the courts below by holding that the title had not been lost by adverse delivery before the suit was filed. The question as regards whether a sale effected by a manager in regardto properties belonging lo the temple is void, and the decision was based on the facts proved in relation to this aspect of the matter.

The appellants, who were the partners of a firm Apsara Theatre, Gandhi Nagar, Jammu, had been declared to be the sole licensee in respect of the Apsra Theatre. The District Magistrate rejected the said request by an order dated April 21, 1979. The State Government preferred an appeal before the High Court against the order passed by the District Magistrate directing suspension of cinema shows in the Theatre premises of Apsala Theatre. A single Judge of the High court dismissed the writ petition holding that the licence could not be granted to a licensee who was held responsible under the Act and the Rules for due compliance with all the terms and conditions of the licence and answerable to the licensing authority for all commissions and omissions in the Cinema premises, he may be saved from any prosecution or other action under law in the capacity of licensee of the Theatre. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the District magistrate had no power under the provisions of the Act to suspend a licence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The licensing authority has no jurisdiction to suspend the licence. [623C] 2. Section 6 F of the Jammu and Kashmir Cinema (Regulation) Act, 1978 provides that no person shall be disqualified for being chosen as or for being associated with any exhibition of cinematographs in a cinema theatre unless he is held responsible by the licensee for all commission and omissions committed by others in the said premises. [723D] 3. Section 7 F of Jammu and Srinagar (Regulation of Trade) Act 1978 provides for suspension of licence pending enquiry. The power to suspend or cancel a licence is conferred only by Section 6F of the J&K Cinema (Control of Trade & Commerce) Act 1977. [824E] 4. Section 8 F of J& K Cinema ( Control of Trade and Commerce) Rules, 1979 provides that every person who has been declared as sole licensee shall be liable to pay a fine which may extend to five hundred rupees or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one month. The only other provision in the Act is that the licensing Authority has no power to suspended a licence pending inquiry. [820G] 5. Section 9 F of Act provides that the State Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, make rules for regulating the conduct and business of any person or class of persons in the performance of its functions under this Act. The rules made thereunder provide for the grant of licences to persons who are holding a licence for exhibition of films in the cinema theatre known as Apsar Theatre. [822G] 6. Section 10 F provides that a licence may be suspended or cancelled by the licensing authorities if it is proved that the holder of such licence has contravened any of the provisions contained in the Jammu & Kashmir Cinema Act, 1977 and the rules made there under. The words "any person" occurring in section 9F of J & K Cinema Act must be read as "any other person". [822H] 7. Section 11 F of R & K cinema (Control) Rules 1979 provides for the suspension or cancellation of a licence granted to persons holding a valid licence. It is not necessary that a licensee should have been given an opportunity before passing any order under section 6F(1)(a). The licensing authorities have no power either under the statute or the rules to suspend such licence. They have also no power in the matter of suspension or revocation of the licences. [823A B] 8.

The appellants, who were the owners of the mills and the factory in question, applied to the Custodian for cancellation of the lease granted by him under section 12 of the (XXXI of 1950), hereinafter referred to as the Act. The respondent issued a notice to the appellants on 13 2 1954, calling upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled and why they should not pay their dues. On 13 2 1951 the appellants appeared before the respondent and contended that he had systematically committed breaches of the various terms on which the properties bad been leased to them, and called upon them, to showcause why the leases should not not be terminated and why their should not been evicted. The Custodian rejected this contention. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice. The High Court held that section 12 applied only to properties of the evacuee by reason of the sale in favour of the appellants, and that the notice was to that extent without juris,diction, and therefore the notice, Exhibit C, was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under that section. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The provisions of section 12 are unqualified and absolute and that power cannot be abridged by reference to the provision that it could be exercised "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". [982 E] (2) The notice Exhibit C was to a limited extent without jurisdiction. [984 B] (3) The notices, Exhibit D, were to a restricted extent without any jurisdiction and that therefore the notices, Exhibits C, and C, were ultra vires. [ 984 A] (4) The Custodian had the power under section 10 to cancel the lease in favour o the appellants.

[924E] 3:3 The Board has power under Section224 of the Constitution to question its judgment or order of any superior court which is not otherwise provided by the Act. [1125C] 5.3 The High Court was right in holding that it was not appropriate for the Board to exercise the powers conferred by Section 9(1) of the land Revenue Act in view of the fact that the State having not filed an appeal under section 225 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and revision under Section 230 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, the High Court could not have set aside any part of that order which has gone against the State and in his favour.
