The appellant was working as a newspaper establishment. The State Government issued an order on the basis of recommendations of Justice Palekar award. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order before the High Court in a writ petition filed by him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the law reports do not carry any news and information. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The expression `newspaper ' as defined in the Act includes not merely `public news or comments on public news but also `comments on public News and information'. [723C] 1.2 The expression 'newspapers' is defined by section 2(b) of the Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955 as any working journalist, and includes such other class of printed periodical work as may be notified in this behalf by the Central Government in the Official Gazette. [724D] 1:3 The expression "news paper ' means any printed periodical worked containing public news or comment on public newspaper and includes any other class thereof which is interested. It is significant that the expression `public newspaper' has to be understood in its ordinary sense as meaning a newspaper which may after some time cease to be a newspaper and become a book of reference. [824E] 1 :4 The expression ''news Paper ' means newspapers" which are public bodies and these are matters in which the public is interested, but even if it is possible to have two opinions on the construction of the provisions of the Act the one which advances the object of the legislation and is in favour of the employees for whose benefit the Act is passed has tobe accepted. [924F] 1.:5 The expression ̳news newspaper ' as understood in the ordinary sense means any newspaper, which may during some time come into existence or become a newspaper. It includes also `public newspapers'. [925A] 1.?4 The definition of `new' in the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, is not exhaustive. It covers only two categories of printed publications. The first category consists of publication of the recent events which have taken place in the Supreme Court or in the High Courts which are Public bodies and those which are private bodies and the other which are interested. [1025B] 1.(a) The expression ‘news newspapers ' as used in section 2 (b) includes not only `public published news but all other places where High Courts are situated, but also every newspaper establishment is interested in them. [1125C] 2.1 In the instant case, the publication of these items by itself may not occupy a substantial part of a law report which may at some time be said to contain news so as to become newspapers. The publication of such recent events by itself cannot be said either to make a law reports or newspaper which might after some period cease to have been a newspaper or become an book of Reference. [1225D] 2.(b) The definition is wide enough to include not merely 'public news' but also 'public newspapers.' [1226E] 3.2 In the present case, there are two opinions which advances a object of improving the conditions of service of the employee of the newspaper establishments and hence even if the publication was in the nature of a newspaper it would be sufficient to make an law report a newspaper within the meaning of section 2 of the act. [1326G] 3.(c) The word 'new' is used in the context of the definition of the expression 'public newspaper '. It does not include `public publication '.

The appellant was a licensee of the respondent. The agreement was described as an agreement of 'leave and licence ' entered into between the respondent on the one hand and the licensor on the other wherein the respondent had been described as the licensee and the recitals therein recite that the licensor was seized and possessed of and was otherwise well entitled as the monthly tenant of the workshop premises situated at 231, Ripon Road, Cooperative Building, Bombay. The appellant filed a suit for eviction against the respondent alleging that he was a sub tenant of his business and had been granted a licence to use and occupy the said premises for the period of five years from 1st September, 1965 till 31st of August, 1970. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the respondent was a tenant and not a licensee. On appeal by the appellant before the Small Cause Court, Bombay, the High Court held that the appellant had failed to prove that he had been a sub tenancy of the premises on 1st February, 1973 under a subsisting agreement for leave and licence. The High Court also rejected the contention of the appellant that the tenant was in occupation of the said property on 1 st February,1973 as there was nothing on record to show that after 31st March, 1966 the leave and Licence agreement between the parties was renewed or any fresh agreement was entered into. It was further held that since the licence was not put an end to by the appellants and that the licensee had approached the licensor to allow him to occupy and use the premises for carrying out his business of workshop for a period of 5 years, he passed an order of eviction against him. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the judgment of the Small Causes Court. The Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no subsisting agreement between him and the licensee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts had erred in interfering with the finding of the trial court that the relationship between the appellant and the respondent did not exist as a mere licence but as a lease. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have failed to appreciate that the real question involved in this case is whether there was any subsisting agreement or not for leave or licence and whether it was a licence or not. [815E] 2.2 In view of the fact that the exclusive possession to which a person was entitled under an agreement with a landlord was coupled with an interest in the property, the agreement would be construed not as a merely licence but a lease; and that is the judgment impugned in this appeal must fail. [916B] 3.1 It is well settled that where it cannot be said that there is no error apparent on the face of the record, the error if any has to be discovered by long process of reasoning, and the High courts should not exercise jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution. In the instant case, the exclusive ownership to which the appellant was entitled was coupled alongwith an interest therein. [716C] 3:2 The respondent had failed in proving that he is a subtenant of the shop premises situated on 1St February, 1972 as there were nothing on records to show whether he was in possession of the same premises under a valid subsisting licence. good deal of submission was made before us that if it was an agreement for licence then this point could be taken in aid of the submission that the Court had jurisdiction, and there was an estoppel. [1016D] 3(a) The respondent was not a sub licensee but a tenant. [1117C] 4.3 In view Of the fact, it was not open to the High Judge to interfere with the findings of the courts below on the ground that there were no error in the judgment.

The appellant company was a registered Company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The State of Rajasthan had merged in India on January 26, 1950. On January 26 1950, the Ruler of the former Jodhpur State passed an agreement for the continuance of the laws in the covenanting State till such time as they were modified by the new State. The appellant company claimed that the Covenant was in its entirety an act of State and that article VI of the Covenant did not apply to it. The High Court held that the agreement continued to be recognized by the old sovereign and reliance was placed on behalf of the appellant on that decision in support of the contention that even if there was any liability of the latter State to meet the liabilities of the merging States, the exemption as provided in the agreement did not confer any right on the company as against the new sovereign. The appeal by special leave was dismissed by this Court. In the appeals before this Court it was contended on behalf Of the appellant that the covenant by which the new Company came into existence was in reality an act or conduct of the new Government and that therefore the exemption could not operate to confer any rights on the appellant as against its new sovereign, for the principle was well settled that there was always recognition of this liability by the former State of Dholpur to be bound by the liabilities arising from the existence of those laws. Held: (i) The agreement was not a law. It was merely an act which clearly applied to the Mills and it was held that there could be no question of recognition by the Union of the right to exemption, if any, under the agreement with the Ruler. [184 D] (ii) The covenant in the Covenant expressly provided for the recognition by a new sovereign and its reliance on the continuance or otherwise that law would prevail and the liability may disappear provided the new law is within the competence of the State legislature and does not transgress the constitutional limitations after the Constitution came into force. The agreement did never confer any power on the Company as against it. [185 E] (iii) The agreements were not a valid agreement. It merely applied to all existing States which eventually became included in it subject always to this that if the new Act was repealed or altered, recognised that it was liable in the same way as would have been the merged State if there had been any liability on the merges State, throughout this process of merger, without change till they were repealed or modified, recognised the rights of the subjects and that the new Central Government assumed liabilities of those States. [186 F] (iv) The Agreement was not an agreement to be regarded as a law and it did not create any right in favour of the company. It only applied to certain territories which eventually were included in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The agreements did not provide for the continuation of laws in those areas, but merely provided that the existing laws would prevail. [187 G] (v) The contract was not one of the contracts of the erstwhile Ruler of Jodhpur State and it could not be enforced by citizens against the old State. It did not become a law if there were any liability arising from such an agreement.

The appellants were the owners of a notified commercial crop in the State of Madras. The appellants purchased the said notified agricultural crops from the sellers and sold them to the sellers. The sellers made an application for permission to sell the said agricultural crops on payment of Rs. 1,000/. The appellant contended that the appellants had not been prevented from doing their business as property, for they could still utilise it for commodities other than the notified crops. Held, that the deduction described as I mahimai ' allowance is a trade allowance and does not operate upon any other payments made which are not trade allowances. The word "mahimi" in section 14 of the Act means a person who has a licence to trade, or business and the other is to hold his property, i.e., the market committee to enforce the provisions of the act. The words "any transaction" in the context of the definition of 'mahemai ' are wide enough to include transactions which are covered either by section 14 or 15 of the Central Act. The term "mahsimai " is a word used in the sense of a word, and it means a thing defined as a thing or a thing which is capable of being construed in its ordinary meaning. It includes not only a person having a licence but also any other person who is entitled to do business. The definition of "moral" in s. 14 of Central Act does not include a person whose trade or business is carried on by him. The expression "mala" in this context means a place where the market is fixed, and the words "machinery" are wide and comprehensive enough to cover transactions which fall within the terms of section 14. The question whether the allowance is allowed to be received by the rules or bye laws framed under that section is a trading allowance depends upon the nature of that deduction. No material has been placed before us to arrive at a definite finding in the present case whether the allowances are permitted to be receive by the Rules or bye law mentioning the " mahmimai" allowance as one not deductible in any transaction. No materials have been placed on record to show that the allowance described as II mahamimai is a profit allowance, within the meaning of section 2(d) of the Income Tax Act.

The appellants were convicted by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to transportation for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the death sentences should be maintained and that those of the other two should be commuted to transportation because of the difference of opinion in the High Court, not only on the question of guilt, but also on the point of sentence, but on the basis of evidence adduced by the prosecution that there was a dacoity at Ramchander 's house. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The conviction of the accused for an offences under section 377 read with Section 34 of Indian Penal code is not based on any evidence and it is well settled that in every case where two Judges concur on the fact of guilt the law directs otherwise. But when appellate Judges differ on that of sentence the matter is always a matter of discretion unless there are compelling reasons. [696 H] (2) The question of sentence must always remain, a matter which depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If two Judges agree on the questions of guilt and differ on the evidence adduced in the case of another Judge concur on that point, it is usual not to impose the death penalty unless there is compelling reasons for depart from this practice in this case and so reduce the sentences of death in the cases of other two Judges also. [596 F] (3) The principle underlying section 377 of the Code does not abrogate or modify that provision. But if appellate Judges agree with the opinion of one Judge, it must always be reasonable to depart from the practice in the matter of sentence unless there were compelling reasons to depart therefrom. [797 C D] (4) The rule of common intention is that when two Judges differ upon the question whether a particular blow was intended to be given or not, they concur because of that difference of opinions in the two courts. If it be accepted that Nilia aimed a blow at Ram chander ''s thigh be so half hearted about it that it did not even hit him; and in Pandurang 's case, though armed with a lethal weapon, he did no more than inflict a comparatively light head injury. There is then the necessary meeting of the minds. There was evidence of enmity on the part of the two who did the actual murder. There were some vague evidence to the effect that there had once been a dacoity in the house and that it was for that reason that they thought to have joined in the attack but had no hand in the killing, and none on the side of the three who did, the actual occurrence. The utmost this shows is that no stick blows were found on the body and that we are prepared to accept.

The petitioner was appointed as officiating Executive Engineer in Class I service on 25.5.1976 and he was compulsorily retired by order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.1976 made under Rule 56(j)(i) of the Fundamental Rules. The petitioner challenged that order for retirement and has claimed payment of remuneration which he would have been entitled to draw upto the normal date of superannuation. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the Government servant officiating in Class II service or post could be retired compulsorily by exercising the power under Rule56(j) (i) after he had attained the age of 50 years on 10.2.1972 and, therefore, on the date of the order he was not entitled to salary and other allowances payable to him from the date o f his normal superannuation. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the petitioner was in Class III service or Class II Service or post and he had entered Government service before attaining the age Of 50 years after he has attained the said age of fifty five years on October 10, 1976 and therefore, he could not be compulsorily retired under Rule 55(j). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The expression "if he is in Class ' I or Class ' II service ' means that he must substantively belong to the two classes of service or posts held on substantive basis. [605B] 2.2 The expression 'temporary hand' has been defined in Rule 56 (j)(ii) as meaning a Government servant who at the relevant time was in class I or class II service, or post is in such service or p ermanent or temporary capacity. It is not necessary that the expression should be confined to service or olution or post as covered by sub clause (i). [606C] 3.1 Rule 56 of the Rules does not apply to Government servants in Class 1 or Class I or Classes II service. The purpose of the sub clauses (i), namely, the Government Servant is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and the classification of Government servants into two categories and sub clause(ii) takes within its sweep those Government servants who at th relevant time were in Class IV service or Post. [706F] 3:2 The purpose behind the sub clause is to conferring power on t he appropriate authority, namely, State Public Works Department in the Ministry of Works and Housing of Government of India and the status of Government servant concerned. If the condi tion indicated in sub clause.(i) is satisfied, namely the Government servants are in Class 11 or Class III Service or posts they can be reverted to the post, if any, on which he has a lien. [806F G] 3 :3 The expression used in Rule 55 (j) is wide enough to include Government servants officiating in class II or Class IV services or posts. [907C D] 4.1 In the instant case, the petitioner had not attained the superannuation age of 60 years by the date he was appointed de novo and could be reverted from the substantive post. The question whether a person who is in class III service can be in Class C or Class 11 service or in Class 12 service or on officiating basis cannot be decided in view of the fact that a Government Servant belonging to a class I service or a post is outside the purview of sub clause. (i); [908F G H] 4:4 The expression `temporary hand" has been used in the context of Rule 56 and it is obvious that the intention behind it is to give power on an appropriate authority.

The appellant Corporation had taken a loan from the Life Insurance Corporation of India for the purpose of construction of a building. The proposal was accepted by the Divisional Manager on 11th January, 1961 and as such there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation. On the death of the deceased, the amount covering two cheques were lying in the deposit and in the suspense account of the Corporation and was not adjusted towards the premium since the proposal was not considered, the terms of acceptance were not fixed and the premium amount required for the proposal. The suit was filed by the plaintiffs respondents claiming a decree for Rs. 1,00,000/ with interest at 18% per annum from 11th February, 1961 till payment. The Trial Court held that there was a concluded contract of insurance between the parties and that the deceased was assured and told by the local agent and the field officer of the corporation that the payment of first premium would amount to acceptance of the proposal if the proposal is not accepted, the term of acceptance was not fixed. On appeal, the High Court held against the appellant Corporation. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The proposal sent by the deceased did not indicate the position alleged by the appellants that there were assurance on behalf of the field officers and local agent to the deceased that the payments of first premiums would amount acceptance of proposal if it was not otherwise accepted. [85G] 2.2 The proposal must be accepted by all concerned authorities of the Life insurance Corporation established that the proposal sent through its acceptance letter dated 11th May, 1961 was for some reason 357 or other not accepted by it. [86B] 3.3 In the instant case there was assurance on the part of the respondent that the amount paid would amount towards the acceptance of a proposal. It was also admitted that the cheque issued towards the first premium was encashed and the appellant corporation had encashed the cheques issued towards premium. The High Court was of the view that having regard to the conduct of the parties, there was an assurance on their part that the repayment of the sum would amount only to the acceptance. [87C] 4.4 In the present case there is no evidence that such could have been the deposition in law. There was a clear admission by the respondent Corporation that the cheques were encashed and that it was never appropriated by it in its accounts and the said premium amount 354 was received by the Corporation without any demur or qualification and that in any event the Corporation must be deemed to have waived by its conduct formality, if any, of sending communication of its acceptance of proposals. [88D] 5. The contention that the respondent corporation had accepted the proposal for Rs Learned Trial Judge was correct. It is not disputed that there is a concluded and valid insurance contract between both the parties namely principal together with interest is paid back to the Corporation by the appellantCorporation. [89E] 6. In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs in this Court.

The appellant company was a registered Company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The respondent company had been carrying on business in coal and coal. It was alleged that the appellant company had entered into an agreement with the respondent for sale of coal and coke. The appellant company contended that the respondent had not paid the price of coal as agreed between them and that the price was not paid by the respondent. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was barred under article 133 (1) (c) since the respondent 's suit was still pending, the order passed in the suit did not finally dispose of the rights of the parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the case. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that an order granting temporary injunction was a final one within the meaning of article 133(1) of the Constitution and therefore, the High Court had erred in holding that an interlocutory judgment even if it decides an issue or issues without finally determining the rights and liabilities of the party in dispute is not a judgment. HELD: The expression "final order" in article 133 means a final adjudication by the Court of the right of the persons in dispute 'in dispute in a suit or proceeding. If the decision on an issue put an end to the suit, the suit or proceedings becomes infructuous as framed and the plaintiffs may have to seek amendment of the plaint to get effective relief, an order which is essentially an interlocutory order may be deemed final for the purposes of article133 (1). [620 E] The expression 'final order' in article 134(1)(c) means a decree. The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti. On March 14, 1975 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed lawfully to the post of Head Clerk prior to his absorption in Government service had to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending Act came into force. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the amendment made by the Amending Acts of 1973 and January 21, 1974. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the panchayat Samiti until he was absorbed in Government Service. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the amendment brought about the amendment by the amending Acts of 1972 and January 25, 1973, was not ultra vires as it did not take away the right to be considered for promotion but only confined its right to appointment to the Panchayat Samitis on the basis of the terms and condition of service. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The amendment brought into the Amending laws of 1973 by the Amendment Act of 1973, which came into effect on June 13 1973, did not affect the right of the appellant to be treated for promotion as a head Clerk in any event. [723B] 2.2 The amendment made in the Amending statutes of 1972 by the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973 was clarificatory in nature and it could not have been taken away by the amendment of the Amending Statute of 1973. [761C D] 3.3 The amendment introduced by the amended Acts of 1974 and January 24, 1973 by which the Amending act had received the assent of the Governor 736 on April 25,1973, being the date on which the Panchayat Parishad lost its power to make appointments to the Panchayats. [763D] 4.4 The appellant was not entitled to be absorbed in the post as aHead Clerk on the date when it purported to do so. [762B] 5.5 The amendment of section 33 of the Act by the impugned Amending Acts did not operate retrospectively and it did take away that right on June 12, 1973 being the day on which it purportedto do, in January 1975 on an Ad hoc basis or in April 1975 on a regular basis. It could not, therefore, have appointed the appellant as ahead Clerk on April 1, 1975 on any regular basis or on April 19, 1975. [769C D; 723A] 6.6 The amendment was clarificatory and it had no retrospective effect. [779B] 7.7 In view of the fact, that the appointment of the respondent to the posts of a Head clerk was without the authority of law, the Government was not bound to absorb him in the posts on which his services were employed by it. The appointment of respondent to such post had to he recognised and protection, despite his having been absorbed in government service. [773G] 8.8 In view Of the fact the appellant had been appointed validly as a Headmaster on an adhoc basis in February 1974 on a permanent basis, the appellant could not be absorbed as a Senior Head Clerk. The order of appointment of a respondent to that post was made without the sanction of law and the Government could not absorb him into the post. [789C] 9.9 In view o the fact of the matter having been placed before the High court, it had not taken away the rights of the parties to the litigation.

All those facts and circumstances must be taken into consideration and on a balancing of the entire evidence it has to be determined whether the property can be said to belong to the temple. It is also clear that the fund was the personal Property of MahantShivshankar Yadav, who in 1921 employed it for the purchase of the Amayl properties devolved on Uma Shankar Yatra. The burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim must be borne by the party making the claim. [677E] 6. In view of the fact that the funds from where a nuDO or temple was acquired constituted his personal property, the income earned by him from these lands cannot be said as property of Math and the image of the idol could not be said that he did not belong to Math or temple or is his personal properties. [678B] 7. The amount of Rs. 30,000 formed part of his personal and exclusive property of Shivshhankar Yatti was not includible in the assessment proceedings. [679C D] 8. The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. They filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification issued thereunder on March 24, 1955. The High Court dismissed the petition and held that the jurisdiction to revise the order had been taken away by virtue of the provisions of section 12(2) and 19 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the power of the Custodian under the , to allot any property to a person or to cancel an allotment made in favour of a person rests on the fact that the property vests in him. HELD: (1) The expression "any property" is not defined in section 2(a) of the , and it includes all properties which are held by the Custodian as his own. [6C D] (2) The definition of evacuee property in section 3(a)(i) of Act, does not include any property which is held or acquired by a person whether such allotment or lease was granted before or after the commencement of the . [6D E] (3) The word "property" in section 4(a), means all properties and rights which are vested in the Custodian. It includes all lands which are evacuee property. [7E H] (4) The words "any person" in clause (i) to (iii) of section 3 of the, include any person who is a displaced person. [8G H] In the instant case, the Custodian by reason of the divesting of the property as from March 24 1955 had become functus officio with respect to it and could not rectify any error made by him in the past in the matter of cancellation of allotment. Sub section (2), therefore, cannot be said that section 19(1) of The Act is completely in conflict with section 10 of the in so far as the question of cancellation is concerned. [9E F] (5) The Custodian has no jurisdiction to cancel a allotment or leases made in his favour. [10G H; 11A] (6) The notification under section 12 of the with respect of any property or class of property would cease to be evacuee property, the displaced person to whom land was allotted "held" the land and was in possession of such property at the date of the publication of the Notification under section 13(1). [11B C] (7) The power of a managing officer or a managing corporation is in conflict With section 10 Of the Act, it permits cancellation only on certain specified grounds and, therefore, it cannot be held that section 18 is completely inconsistent with section 19 of 1954 Act.

The rule is based on the principle that trial of a suit cannot be brought to an end merely because the interest of a party in the subject matter of the suit has devolved upon another during the pendency of the litigation but that suit may be continued against the person acquiring the interest with leave of the Court. On the basis of their seniority, the respondents issued a notification dated October 29, 1979 fixing the age of superannuation of all Government employees, other than in the last Grade Service, from 58 to 58 years. The petitioners challenged the said notification on the ground that it is unreasonable and arbitrary in the circumstances of the case. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the reduction of the age was not justified because it was not arbitrary or unreasonable in the facts and circumstances bearing on the question of fixing the retirement age. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The proviso which conferred a benefit upon Government servants by protecting their conditions of service, cannot be amended so as to empower the Government to alter those conditions to their prejudice and, in any event, they cannot be altered retrospectively so as To take away rights which had already accrued to them. [423C] 2.2 The proviso is not arbitrary and unreasonable in its circumstances. No. The contention of the petitioners that the amendment of February 17, 1983 to Fundamental Rules was made by the State Government in exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution cannot be accepted because it is not unreasonable or unreasonable for reducing the age from 55 to 58. [523D] 2:3 The proviso confers a benefit on Government servants who had already been stagnated in the lower positions due to expansion of educational facilities; that the said recommendation was accepted by the Corporation and consequently, the age Of retirement was raised to 58 with effect from October 29 l 979. It is not reasonable or unreasonable. [525A] 2.(4) The proviso does not confer a benefit which upon Government servant by protecting his conditions of Service, cannot also be amended retrospectively so that to take away right which had accrued to him, the Government may alter those condition to their detriment and, therefore, they can be amended prospectively so asto take away benefits which have already accrued. [500B] 2(5) The reduction of age of retirement from 58 years to 55 in the instant case is not illegal or unreasonable but is based on a recommendation of the one Man Pay Revision Commission appointed by it. No such contention was raised before the High Court and no ground has been made out for increasing the age. [623C D] 2 (6) The second proviso which confers a right upon Government employees by protecting its conditions of services, cannot therefore be amended retrospective so as not to empower Government to altered those conditions. [723D E] 3.1 In the instant cases, the first ground of challenge to the reduction in the age is that the Government had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement; that it felt that raising the age for retirement from 55 years was not a ground for increasing its age of Retirement from 58. The second ground of attack to the reduced age of 55 is that there was no basis at all for reducing age of retire from 58 and that the decision of the Government is bad for a total non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstance bearing on this question of the superannuation, like increased longevityvity. [823E] 2 :3 The second contention of Shri Venugopal challenged the Ordinance on the grounds that it was unreasonable and unreasonable and violative of Article 14 or Article 16 since it is neither arbitrary nor unreasonable in law.

The appellants were dealers in milk, from any source in the State of Haryana. The Sales Tax Officer assessed the appellants to sales tax under section 9(1) of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973 (hereinafter re ferred to as 'the Act '). The appellants contended that the words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later, clause (b) above were clarificatory and not retrospective. The High Court rejected the contention on behalf of the Revenue holding that the word "disves of" was unduly elastic enough to include cases of despatches by a dealer of the manufactured goods otherwise than by way of sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce or in the process of export out of the territory of India within the meaning of section 5(3) of Act. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The words "or despatches the manufactured" used therein i.e. for the manufacture of goods specified in Schedule B should be deemed to have been deleted from the statute. [723C] (2) The word "sale" is not a term of art. It has no different meaning than that of an agreement between two parties. It may be a transfer of property in goods and it may be either by way o sale or otherwise, but it must be a sale in execution of a contract. [823D] (3) The definition includes within the definition of 'turnover " the purchase value of goods liable to tax under the Act on the goods in question when they are sold by a registered dealer for the purpose of (a) local sale; or (b). sale in course of export outside the territory oi India. [820E] (4) The expression "sale in the context of sub section (1)(b) is not to be construed as including any transfer of title in goods by way either of sale, gift, exchange or lease or otherwise. It must be understood in its ordinary sense and it must have a different meaning. [822B] (5) The term "sale " has no relation with the expression "turnover" used under section 5 of the C.S.T. Act. [823A B] (6) The sale of goods is not only as contended for the assessees but also on the hypothesis as to the invalidity of section 9 of the Act. It is a transfer in execution oi s 9(3)(b).

The appellant who was a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1947, passed an order on March 31, 1958, that the goods remained in the sellers ' property till they crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream. The appellant contended that the sales were not oil FOB contracts but were goods which had been exported by him to the buyers on shipment, that is, after they had crossed the custom barrier and therefore no tax was realisable on these sales in view of the provisions of article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. Held: (i) The words " a person " in section 10(b) means a registereddealer to whom he has sold the goods. It is true that the intention of the Legislature is not to levy purchase tax on a person who has given such certificate under section 8(b). But if at the time a declaration of intention is made in the certificate the purchasing dealer had the intention as stated and ultimately he sells to a person whom the certifying dealer has sold goods. The intention of Parliament that there was no circumstance which would justify a conclusion that the parties came to a special agreement that though the sales are on FOB contracts property in the goods passed to the buyer at some point of time before shipment, it cannot strictly be said that the declaration has not been carried out. (ii) The object of the Act is to secure that the declared goods purchased were intended for being despatched by him or by a person to whom the certifies dealer has sells the goods to an address outside the State of Bombay within a period of six months from the date of purchase by the dealer furnishing such certificate. It was not necessary to give a declaration as regards intention of goods being despatched outside the country of Bombay, but it is sufficient if at that time a certificate of intention was made in respect of such goods and the purchasing dealers had the knowledge as stated that they were not 'despatched outside the state of Bombay. (iii) The language used in section 8 has to be interpreted as the time when the customs frontier is crossed and that it must proceed on the basis that the declarations have not been complied with. It would be reasonable to think that if at a time a declared goods are not despatched by some person who is not a registered trader, it can strictly be stated that the persons came to an agreement that although the goods were not despatched within the State, they had sold the said goods to a registered dealers for despatch of the goods outside the territory of Bombay and so the sales must be held to have taken place "in the course of export" and the exemption under article 286 (1)(a) will come into operation. The words ' a person ' in section 5(b), therefore, mean a registered manufacturer to whom a certificate has not already been complied. (iv) The word ' a ' in Section 10(a) means " a registered ' dealer to whom goods are intended to pass and does pass on the shipment of the said articles." (v) The expression 'person ' in s. 10(c) is used in the sense that it will be reasonable for think that the person who sells the imported goods should not be liable for having made a false declaration. It may also be that if ultimately the actual despatch is made by some other person who was not a Registered dealer, it would not be possible to say that he has purchased the goods but he sold them to an agent who is a registered owner for despatch outside the Province of Bombay or that he sells them to a dealer who is neither a registered nor a registered seller. (vi) The term 'person " in s 10(d) means ' a registered person to which he has given a certificate under s 8(a).

The appellant was a married woman and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 400/ for the mother for her subsistence, taking due note of the fact that the respondent had transferred the suit premises to the appellant and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. The Magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance held that the appellant was not a wife, dismissed the petition in allowance of the appeal. On appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: (1) Section 125(3)(b) is an enabling provision enacted to ameliorate the economic condition of neglected wives and discarded divorcees. The object of section 127(3) is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the parties. [81 E] (2) Section 127(4) does not confer a right on the husband to claim under section 125 towards a divorced wife except on proof of payment of a sum stipulated by customary or personal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance. The language used in sub section (3)(a) is clearly indicative of the intention that the wife should be made out if the hurdle of section 125(4). [81 F] (3) Section 126(3), as it stood before the amendment, was not intended to confer a special right on her husband. The words "wife ' includes a woman who has been divorced by her husband and has not remarried. The word "wife" in sub Section (3), is clearly suggestive of the idea that she should be given with wherewithal to maintain herself.

[602C] 3.3 The Rent controller has to deal with this incidentally but this is not one of direct issues before the Rent Recovery Tribunal as well as fixing the standard rent in accordance with the provisions o the Act and then fades out of the picture. In an application under section 12, the court of Small Cause and to consider and determine afresh the issue as to whether the applicant is a tenant or landlord of, the building and (2). What the fair value of the property should be in accordance wi th law. [643E] 4. The answer, in our opinion, has to be in the negative. There is no doubt that, since an order passed totally without jurisdiction, though it has became final as a result of a revision under section 65 C, it will have to pass a decree in favour of the LIC on the basis of the correct fair rent fixed by the Appellate Tribunal. If, and only if, this relationship exists between the parties, the rent controller steps in for a limited purpose to determine what the fair rents are and then foades out the picture, it would have to passed a decree on the ground that there is no relationship of a landlord and tenant and therefore, impliedly excluded from the purview of the civil court. The petitioner was given a provisional seniority list on an integrated seniority list, a position to which he objected. He was also given an opportunity to object to the provi sional list before the final list was prepared. The respondents were not heard after the final lists were published. They filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the provisional list. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioner was entitled to an opportunity of making a representation with regard to the two points urged by him before the Court on the merits and demerits of the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the respondents were entitled to a hearing before the provisional seniority lists were still to be prepared after hearing objections, and that the writ petitions should not be entertained as the final seniority list had already been published. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The principle recognised in Shankariah 's case (supra) is not applicable to such a case. [623B] 1.2 The petitioner respondent was entitled only to an ad hoc or temporary appointment and that he should have a further opportunity against even a final seniority lists. If the Central Government had acted properly according to the provisions of the Act, we are of the view that a Court cannot go into the merits or otherwise of equation of posts which is a matter within the province of the Courts to lay down what are in the principles to be adopted for purposes of equation. [723C] 1:3 The petitioner was not entitled to any opportunity against the final gradation list on some such grounds of invalidity, those grounds have to be shown to exist. If he was to have that opportunity the list would not really be final but only provisional or preliminary. Roy 's Case (supra), the opportunity afforded was to be given before the publication of the final select list. [761D] 1 :4 The petitioner had no further opportunity, and it could not possibly be said that he did not have a second opportunity against him. If a particular decision is mala fide or arrived at on totally irrelevant and extraneous consideration ations, such a decision can be interfered with by Courts. [763F] 2.5 In the instant case, the petitioner respondent Dr. R.D. Nanjiah was not able to make out any ground for interference with the final order of the High court. [762B] 3. The petition was dismissed on the ground that it was premature as the provisional gradation list had been still to remain in force. [764C] 4.1 In view of the special circumstances of the present case, there is no merit in this appeal and the same is accordingly dismissed.

The petitioners in both the writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of cut and polished diamonds. The petitioners in these two writ petitions were granted Additional licences to Export Houses under the Additional Licences category as per para 176 of Import Policy for the period 1978 79 excluding those items which were banner in the policy for the periods 1978 79 and those which have been specifically banned in the prevailing Import Policy, 1985 88. The respondents in both these writ petitions had imported rough diamond and export goods of cut & polished rough diamond. The Additional licences issued to them were valid for a period of 12 months and they contained the following endorsement: "This licence in valid for import of items permissible to Export House under the Import & Export Policy 1988 91 excluding those articles which havebeen specifically banned under the Export Policy,1985 88, pursuant to and subject to the decision of the Supreme Court dated 5.3.1986 in M/s. Rajnikant Brothers case (supra) and had been specifically exempted from the provisions of Import & Exports Policy 1978 89, pursuant thereto and subject thereto the decision on the issue of Additional licences under the import & Export policy 1988 91 was quite different from those contained in the Import and Export Policy for 1978 79. The petitioner in both writ petitions is a partnership firm carrying on trade business of export of rough and polishing diamonds, which were banned in 1977 78. In other words, under the Imports & Exports policy 1988 79 Additional licences are to be given on the basis of one third of the f.o.b. value of the exports made during 1986 87 or earlier periods have been denied the facilities which have already expired in the meantime. The contention of the petitioners is confined to sub para (10) of para 218 of Import and Exports Policy 1988 89 and the Export Houses who were issued Additional licences on or after April 1, 1988, under Import & export Policy 1978 91 are also entitled to a similar relaxation. In the writ petition filed by the respondents it has been contended that under Import and export policy 1988 80 Additional licences were to be granted on the ground of exports made in 1977 79 and that they contained no similarity between the petitioners who have been granted Additional Licences on the date of import and export effected during 1986 88. It is further submitted that under the Foreign Trade Policy 1978 79, Additional licences could be given only on the strength of exports actually made and the value of such Additional licence was only 10 to 12% of the export turnover. The appellants in both cases are also similarly circumstanced as Export Houses which were granted additional licences under Import/ Export Policy 1978 80. In respect of Additional Licences issued to the petitioners, it has further been urged that there is no similarity with the petitioners whose exports have been made during the year 1977 78 and in subsequent years and obtain Additional licences for a much lesser value under the said policy. The learned Additional Solicitor General submitted that there was difference between the conditions for grant of such licences under import & export policy 1978 79 which were quite different and therefore, the petitioners cannot avail the same and are able to import the goods which can be so imported under the prevailing import Policy. In view of the fact that the matter has been pending in this Court and the Additional licences granted to the petitioner have expired in meanwhile we consider it appropriate that the period of validity of the said licences should be extended so that the petitioners can avail the benefit of the same.

The appellant, a manufacturer of excisable goods, was manufacturing the goods. The appellant manufactured the goods in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer to the assessee. The price of packing materials including those supplied by the appellant was included in the assessable value only when the packing is either manufactured by the assessee or is purchased by the manufacturer or by the supplier to the asses see to the buyer, in respect of all other costs of packing, the cost of such pack ing would have to be added to the price except where the packing was either manufactured at the factory gate or is sold by the purchaser to the purchaser. The Tribunal held that at the time of removal, goods were delivered from the factory in packed conditions and the container was not returnable to by the buyers, there fore, the value had to be included in assessable value. It was further urged that on a correct interpretation of section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act, the costs of pack ing could be included In the assessable Value only when it is sold at the gate of the factory and not the manufacturer. The contention that the cost price of the drums should be added in the value of the 985 excisable goods was rejected by this Court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The cost of packing envisaged in section 4 (4)(D)(i), is repugnant to the very scheme of section 3. [520E] 2.1 In cases where the manufacturer supplies the drums and charges the customers separately therefore, under section 4, the Cost of such packing would have been included in that value if necessary, by addition to the sale price, except only where the packaging is durable in nature and is returnable by such buyer to a manufacturer. [620F] 2 2.2 The cost price for which the goods are sold at a factory gate is to be taken as the assessable valuation of the excisable goods. [721B] 3.3 In cases wherein the cost would be included, in the price, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market. The cost Of such packaging includes the cost cost of the packing as also the cost thereof. [821C] 4.4 The cost cost envisaged in Section 4(3)(d) does not in clude within its ambit the cost o f packing which was returnable by it to the manufacturer when the packaged is supplied by him to the importer. The manufacturer levies an additional charge for such packing where the price is intrinsally and inevitably ancillary to placing it on the Market. [921F] 4(5)(d). In cases, where the cost is of a durable nature and returnable by t he buyer to his assessee, in all other cases the cost should be included. The "cost of such Packing" referred in section 3 does not mean that while generally the normal price for the sale of the goods is to include cost of packaging which is incidental to putting the excisable article in question, the price of such packages would haveto be added. [1021F G] 4.(6) The cost for packing envisaged under section 3 is repugnant only to the scheme of Section 4. If this question is answered in the affirmative, then in respect o the goods so sold, thecost of the pack ing will have to include in the valuation of such goods where such goods are delivered at the place of removal in packed Condition. [1121F H] 5. The expression "value" in section 2(4) does Not in cluding within its scope mean that in cases where a manufacturer supplies any drums and charge the customers specifically, in terms of sub clause (ii), the cost for such packings shall be included therein.

The appellant was a private Devasthan and a public religious trust. The temple was a public charitable trust. It was a managed institution of the deity. The founder also intended that regular Bhajan, Kirtan and worship shall be conducted by the saints in succession nominated by the reigning saint. The Sanad being an ancient Royal grant is a very important piece of evidence to show that though Sakharam Maharaj had already been succeeded by Guru Govindbuwa and the latter by Balkrishnabuwa, the land had been held in the year 1860 61 in the name of the Devasthan. In accordance with this theory, it has been held that when property is dedicated for the worship of a family idol, it is a private and not a public endowment. The learned District Judge reversed the decision of the Charity Commissioner by his order dated October 16, 1959, and declared the Sansthan to be a private property and not as a public trust. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Sansthan was a Private temple and it was also transferred to the Shishya Adhikari to maintain it as its own property. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The dedication of an endowment is obscure and no direct oral evidence is available, the Court will have to decide whether a property is a public or private trust. [723 E] 2.1 In order to facilitate worship by the public, the emphasis is that regularhants, Kritan and temple are entitled to worship at the shrine of the idol as per tradition. The object and purpose for which the trust was created, the contribution of the public to all intents and purposes, as a whole. [823 F] 2:2 In orderto facilitate worship through the public the contribution Of the public is to be seen whether a particular temple is a religious endowment or not. If it is proved that the property has always been treated as trust property even by the Adhikari saintts and the Adhikaris or the disciples who succeeded one after the other were not owners but trustees of the property, the dedication of the private nature of the trust, the object and purposes for which it was created must be held to have been proved. [820 E] 3.3 The existence of a public temple is obscurity and no indirect evidence is present. [824 G] 4.4 In order that each case of endowment as to its character depends on the particular history. tradition and facts, the presence of the above features in the instant case lead to the inescapable conclusion that Shri Vithal Rukhamai Sansthan at Amalner was a Public Trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act. [825 C] 5.4 The dedication by the founder is obscuring and no direction oral evidence was available, it was never treated as private property. While each case has been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the manner in which the property had long been used by the Public, the contributions of the Public to all Objects and purposes are all important elements in determination of the question whether a public institution is a temple or not, the nature of devolution of the properties, are all vital elements in deciding the question Whether a property was a religious trust or not? [820 G] 5:5 The dedication is obscures and no directly oral evidence has been available. The mere fact that the endowment was in favour of an idol cannot be said to be conclusive proof of dedication on documentary evidence. [828 A] 6.6 In order for deciding whether a temple is private or public endowment, it must be proved that it has always got its character determined by the usage of the temple and the gifts were made with the object of maintenance of the worship.

The petitioner was arrested and detained in jail in execution of a warrant issued under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 for the recovery of arrears of land revenue. The Additional Collector issued a certificate to the Additional Collector on the 7th June 1955 directing him to recover from such defaulter the amount specified therein as if it were an arrear of land Revenue. The petitioner challenged the validity of the order of detention before the High Court in a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition and held that section 46(2) was violative of article 14 of the constitution, and that the provisions of section 46 (2) were not violative of articles 14 and 19 of theConstitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the impugned order of the High court was void under article 13(1) of the , and that section 13 had been amended by Act No. V of 1955, and the warrant of arrest issued against the petitioner was void as being violative of Article 14 of Constitution. Held: (i) The provisions of sections 46(1), 46(3) and 46(4) are not violative either article 19 or article 21; (ii) The impugned order is not valid under article 19(1)(f). It is a well settled principle that the validity or invalidity of an order passed by a competent authority cannot be challenged on the ground of its being illegal. The provisions in section 46 are not, in terms, concerned at all with the recovery and it can be done easily by suitably amending section 46; (iii) The language of section 13 is clear and unambiguous and there is no scope for any intendment or implication from the words "any person" occurring in section 13(2). The provisions are not intended to operate as a bar on the exercise of power under article 14. The words "the Collector may forward to the Collector a certificate under his signature specifying the amount of arrears due from an assessee, and "the collector shall proceed to recover the certified amount as if he were an officer of Income tax". The words 'any person' occurring in sections 46 and 47 are not used in the sense that they are intended to cover all cases in all States. The word 'shall be construed as meaning 'may ' in a particular manner, but it is only when there is some ambiguity or doubt which is likely to affect the validity,ability of an action taken by the Collector that the Collector can proceed to take action under section 46. The language used in section 47 is not intended for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions contained in sections46 and 47. The object of the section is to give effect to all the laws on the subject which are applicable to the recovery, of income tax demand. It is only where there is any ambiguity or dispute which is capable of being resolved by a court that the matter can be referred to the court for determination of the question whether the provisions in sections 47 and 47 should be read into section 46 and not otherwise. The purpose of the provision is to provide for the detention of all defaulters for the same period in all cases, in all courts in India. It cannot be said to be unreasonable for the Union to adopt, for the purposes of recovery of its public demand from defaulters of each State, the same mode of recovery (1) ; , 157. The section is not violative by article 14 or article 19 because it denies equal protection of laws on a par with the defaulter outside the City of Bombay, for he can be detained for a longer period of time. It can be exercised easily by suitable amendment in section46(2), so as to provide that if there be any vice of discrimination in the State laws that vice cannot but be regarded as having crept into section 47(2); and (iii).

The respondents were the trustees of the Port of Bombay. The Trustees, therefore resolved that the shore crew at the Alexandra Docks should work for 8 hours and that there should be a variable recess of one hour and overtime of three hours should be paid. The workmen filed a reference before the Central Government Industrial Tribunal under section 10(2) of the . The Tribunal held that the notices were not valid and directed the appellants to pay wages for overtime and for hours of rest in the work day of the workman. On appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: (1) There is clear antinomy between hours of work and intervals of rest. A working day of 12 hours is thus made up of hours of duty. The check is found in the latter part of Rule 25(1) which says that the maximum number of hours for rest shall break up the hours of overtime worked in a week. It will also be noticed that the interval for rest has not been specified. [815E F] (2) There are clear antInomy between days of work, and intervals for rest in that manner on any particular day can be taken without paying overtime if the total number of days in the week does not exceed 48. The workers at the Prince 's and Victoria Docks work in a different way and their case cannot be compared with that of the Flotilla Crew or the crew at 12 hours shifts, but at theince 's, and VictoriaDocks there is 2 hours' overtime only. [915B] (3) The workers are entitled to three hours ' overtime if they owing to the nature of work there is difficulty in giving the intervals for remaining rest. They are, therefore, entitled to one hour ' overtime as provided under section 55 they shall not spread over more than twelve hours on any day. [1015B C] (4) The number of workers in a factory shall be so arranged that inclusive of his intervals for part, if any, it shall not increase the spread over to 12 hours. [716C D] (5) The total number Of hours of worked in an week shall be 48 (8 hours per day for rest). They are also entitled to two hours ' holidays if required to work beyond the 9 hours on each day and work up to 9 hours in a twelvehour shift. There is no clear anteomy between the hours 8 and 12 hours in which the workmen is either made to work or the interval is not specified. The crew at their Prince ' and Victoria Cocks work are, however, entitled for three hours' holidays if they attend to rest on any days. [616E F; 917A] (6) The provisions of section 13 fixes the number of hour in a normal working day and this number is inclusive of one or more specified intervals. There are no words in the scheme which indicate that the hours for work in an adult worker in a Factory shall break down the hours, if owing to his nature there is difficulties in giving intervals for endless rest over 12 hours on every day. The provisions in section 13 fixing the number and hours of working (which cannot exceed 9) are not intended to be exhaustive of the circumstances under which the notice of the interval was given by specifying a day in advance the hours. There can be no doubt that the legislature has used the word 'inclusive' in the context of the scheme of the compels the inclusion of an hour of rest and spread the 8 hours or 9 hours of the work. [936G H; 916A B] (7) The words 'inclusive of the intervals of hours ' in a 12hour shifts, are not meant to be illustrative but only illustrative. It is not possible that the number should not exceed 9.

The appellant was the tenant of a building let out on June 25, 1976. The accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by the Nagar Palika Ghaziabad with effect from October 1, 1976 and it was contended that as till the matter was pending in the High Court 10 years have not been completed and therefore the benefit of the provisions of Section 20 will be available to the appellant but looking to the language of Sections 39 and 40 of the Act it appears that during the pendency c.f the litigation even of 10 years had not elapsed even if the date of completion is taken to be 1. But this contention was raised on behalf of the respondents that as during the period of 10 year have not elapsed, appellant will be entitled to protection of the provision of Section20 and therefore it was submitted that it is well settled that if during the proceedings 10 years has elapsed even though the date Of completion is taking to be the starting point for computing the period for 10 years in view of the language used in Section 39 and the language thereof it appears clear that the construction put by the appellant on the suit premises was not correct. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The words of Section 2(2) are very wide and they do not cover a suit pending on the date when the first assessment was made and so far as this question is concerned it will be clear that during this pendency c., the protection will be applicable to the present appellant but in Vineet Kumar 's case (supra) this Court took the view that if after the commencement of the tenancy the tenant has not elapsed the tenant will be entitle to the benefit under this Act because according to him the appeal will be a continuation of the suit and therefore he is entitled to the advantage of the Section even if within 10 years he is not entitled to any protection under the Act. [912D] 1.2 The language of this section is clear that for a newly constructed building the provisions contained in sub section (2) of Section 39 will not apply for 10 year and therefore they will not be applicable and it is clear from the language employed in the Explanation that during pendency c, the protection would be available if within the language Of Section 39 the appellant is entitled only to the benefits of the section even if he has come to this conclusion the Court also considered the language in Section39 and it observed: "Further, in order to attract Section 39(2), the suit must be pending on this date and not thereafter. In coming to this finding the Court further considered the words of sub clause (2). The contention advanced by the learned counsel could not be accepted as it is very clear from language of the Explanation which is applicable to a suit filed on 23rd of March, 1974 long after the enforcement of the Rent Act and in coming to the conclusion that during 10 years there has elapsed between the date on which the first suit was filed and 10 years expired. [1012E F] 1:3 The words "from the date as indicated in Explanation 1 and" are very clear and therefore, it appears to be very clear that even if it is held that the rights of the parties have to be determined in respect of the date On which the suit was instituted still because of the wording of Section39(2)(1) it appears from this Act that it applied I only to a case pending on 23 rd March, 1975 but the suit giving rise to the instant appeal is continuation of this suit and if within that period the protection is available to him then he will be eligible to the protection under this section.

The appellant was a thika tenant in respect of certain lands. The respondent No. 1 was the owner of certain land and had been cultivating the same for several years. On the date when the appeal of the respondent No 1 was disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, the rights of the parties were governed by the Thika Tenancy Act of 1949. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent on the ground that he was not entitled to the benefit of the Calcutta Thika tenancy Act, 1949 as amended finally by an Act of 1953 and that the provisions of section 4 of the Act would be applicable. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was not liable to ejectment in the absence of any grounds therefor in the notice to quit in accordance with section 3 of the Ordinance as it stood before the commencement of the said Act; but he dismissed the suit holding that the respondent had failed to file a suit but applied to the controller for an order in that behalf. The High Court held that at the time when the appellant came into force, he was entitled to protection under section 4(2) of the West Bengal Thika Amendment Ordinance, 1952 and that section 4 did not apply to this case. The appellant was appointed as a Section Officer in the pay scale of Rs.400 750 and ten posts in the scale of pay Rs.500 1,000. The State Government issued an order dated January 2, 1986 granting the higher pay scale to the appellant. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court which dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the principle of "equal pay for equal work" has no application in comparison to Bench Secretaries Grade I and II with Section Officers. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The principle of 'equal pay' is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. If it has a rational nexus with the object to be sought for, as reiterated before a certain amount of value Judgment of the administrative authorities who are charge with fixing the pay scales has to be left with them and it cannot be interfered with by the Court unless it is demonstrated that either it is irrational or based on no basis or arrived mala fide either in law or in fact. [319D] 2. The classification made under the Rules, therefore, cannot be said to be violative of the right to equality guaranteed under Article 14 of the Constitution. [419B] 3. The High Court has completely overlooked the criterion provided under the rules framed by the Chief Justice for the purpose of entitlement to higher pay scales. The criteria provided under Rule framed by him is as follows: "Bench Secretary 26.38 Fifty two posts of Bench Secretaries, Grade I, and the designation of rest Bench Secretaries grade II and the posts of Additional Secretary Grade II will be of the same duties and responsibilities. The entitlement to lower pay scale has to depend on the nature of duties and functions and the fact that every Honble Judge will have one Private Secretary in the scales. [519D E] 4. The claim of Bench Secretary for giving them pay scale admissible to Section Officers is therefore, not on the basis of seniority alone but on the principle o f equality enshrined under Article 16 of the Consti tution of India. [620B] 5. The question is whether there can be two grades with different pay scales in the cadre of BenchSecretary who are doing the same or similar work or duties. If this answer is in the affirmative, it will be open to the Court if it is shown that either there is a difference between the two posts and the quality of work may differ. [720C] 6. The nature of duty and responsibilities and the facts that every order passed by those officers who are charges with fixing pay scales have to be seen in the first place. If the High court has completely ignored the criterion laid down under the Rule, it cannot claim as of right the payscale admissible to section Officers. [820D] 7. The Court has totally overlooked the criteria provided in the Rules. Therefore, the principle Of "equal Pay for equal Work" has to apply in comparison with Bench Secretaries who are working in the same cadre of persons performing the same and have to control over its subordinates. [921E] 8. The pay scale recommended by the Pay Commission is as per the rules. The scale of Grade I is Rs.1600 2950 to both the grades of Bench Stenographers Grade II and that merit will be evaluated by a competent authority. Therefore the principle laid down in the said judgment cannot be applied to the case on hand. [1021E F] 9.

The appellant was a Municipality under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961. The respondent I can exercise only such powers to levy property tax as the Municipal Corporation or the Municipal Council had under the provisions of the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act 1956, or the Madhya Madhya Pradesh Panchayats Act, 1962, or any other law for the time being in force. The appellant was assessed to property tax by the Municipal Commissioner on the basis that the respondent I could exercise only those powers which were vested in the State Government under section 127A of the Municipalities Act and section 135 of the Municipal Corporations Act respectively. The Municipal Commissioner passed an order directing the respondent 1 to pay a sum of Rs. 2,000 as penalty for the period from April 1, 1976 to March 31, 1977. The appeal filed by the appellant was dismissed by the High Court. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the levy of property tax was not in conflict with the power conferred under section 69(d) of the Act of 1973 and that the imposition of property taxes was invalid as the State Legislature had no competence to pass a law on the subject and the State legislature had no jurisdiction to impose that tax without following the procedure prescribed by sections 129 and 133 of the aforesaid Acts. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred by section 69 (d) is in conflictwith the powers conferred by the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act on the Union Government pursuant to the declaration made by Parliament in respect of a declared industry and that it was not possible for the State Legislatures to pass any law on that subject and to ensure rational and scientific utilisation of coal resources. The exercise of taxing power under section69(d), is therefore not in contravention with the provisions contained in section 69 of the said Act. [520 E] 2. The property tax is imposed by respondent 1 under section 126A of a Municipality Act or section 135 thereof, which were introduced by an amendment made after the enactment of section 69. It was held by this Court that the ownership rights could be validly acquired by the State government under the State Act and that since sugar was a declared Industry under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951, Parliament alone was competent to pass such a law. [620 E F] 3. The Constitution of India is an organic document which has been enacted for the purpose of providing for the development and administration of Special Areas through Special Area Development Authorities, Section 64 of the Indian Companies Act, 1956, provides that for the purposes of taxation, the Madhya Nadu Municipalities Act 1961 or theMadhya Pradesh Municipalities Corporation Act, 1963, or a Panchayat, as the case may be, shall, in relation to the special area and as from the date the Special Area development Authority undertakes the functions under clause (vi) or clause (vii) of section 68 cease to exercise the powers and perform the function and duties which the Special Areas Development Authority is competent to exercise and perform under the Act. The State Legislature has no competence, therefore, to pass an order imposing property tax without Following the procedure laid down by sections 128 and 133. [720 E H] 4. The properties tax are imposed by the respondent1 under section 125A of that Act on "buildings and lands owned by or vesting in the Union government". The property taxes are levied by respondent I under section 124A of Municipalities Act. Section 127A(2) of Municipalities (Amendment) Act provides that: Notwithstanding anything contained in the Madhya Pradan Adhiniyam, 1961 or any law for time being inforce, the State shall not apply to the Korba Special Area for the said purposes. [820 E G] 5.

The appellant was granted a lease of the land to the respondent on July 1, 1945. The lease was for a period exceeding one year and it was not enforceable against the Government. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the lease. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the lease had been granted subsequent to July 1 1945, and that as the lease was only for a limited period, it was neither enforceable against nor illegal under any law in force at the time when the notified date, i.e., July 1 1944, and therefore, the termination of the appellant 's leasehold rights could not be done under the third proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The appellants contended that the respondent had created a right in favour of the appellants by virtue of section 20 (2), and that the provisions of sub section (2) of section 18 were not applicable to them, as they did not create any right in any land (whether by way of lease or otherwise) including rights in any forest, mines or minerals, quarries, fisheries or ferries, the transaction was not void. Held: (i) The words " such rights" in the third clause of section 2(1)(a) of Act, are not confined to those rights created before the notified day but only to those right which were created after July 1 1946, and if they are for a duration exceeding one years, they would be valid and enforceable by or against the person in whose favour such right had been created by reason of section 21(1). The words 'such rights' in the second proviso refer to the rights created after the 1st day of July 1945 for a term not exceeding oneyear. [47 D] (ii) The creation of rights after July, 1946, is by the force of the second Proviso itself, void as against the State without any further necessity for any overt act to be done by the Government to avoid the same. If any condition was intended to be super imposed on the right of the Government, it must comply with the conditions laid down in the fourth proviso. [48 E] (iii) The existence of a right created after August 1 1945 is by virtue only of section 3, clause (10), of the Estates Land Act, and not any further need for any positive act to have been done by a landholder on or after July1 1945, if it relates to the private land of the landholder within the meaning of section 4.
